title: Paid family and medical leave by state
methodology: We built this in October 2026. For every state with a paid family and medical leave law, we read the state program's own website (benefit amounts, how many weeks, who qualifies, job protection and how to apply) and the law itself, and compared them with the National Partnership for Women & Families' April 2026 chart and a February 2026 benefits-industry summary. Where they disagree, we use the state's own information and explain the difference in the state's notes. For voluntary programs we read each state's law. For states with no program, we used national trackers updated through July 2026, checked 2025 and 2026 bills in many legislatures directly, and read each state's laws on unpaid pregnancy and parental leave. 'Paying' means benefits are paid now; 'enacted' means the law passed but benefits start later; 'voluntary' means an opt-in state plan or a law that lets insurers sell family leave coverage to employers. Bonding weeks are paid weeks to bond with a new child. Pregnancy recovery weeks are the legal maximum for your own pregnancy- or childbirth-related health condition; the usual amount is often shorter, so we also give the agency's typical guidance. The weekly maximum is a ceiling, and most people get less. Several states changed their maximum in mid-2026 (Rhode Island, Oregon, Colorado and Maine in summer, DC on October 1), and most reset on January 1, 2027, so check with your state program before you plan around a number. For the 35 states without a paid leave program, in October 2026 we also checked four workplace laws in each state's statutes, administrative code, civil rights agency and state HR rules, with A Better Balance, NCSL and the U.S. Department of Labor's Women's Bureau as cross-checks: pregnancy accommodations, pumping at work, paid parental leave for state employees, and laws letting insurers sell family leave insurance. Where we checked and found nothing, the page says so. For the 13 programs paying now, the benefit calculator uses each agency's 2026 formula, and we tested it against the agency's own worked examples, benefit tables or calculator results; where an agency publishes none (Massachusetts and Rhode Island, and some amounts for New Jersey, New York and Delaware), against amounts worked out from its published rule.

fieldGuide.status: paying = benefits paid now; enacted = law passed, benefits later; voluntary = opt-in state plan (NH, VT) or insurance-market law; none = no program
fieldGuide.pregnancyRecoveryWeeks: statutory maximum for own pregnancy/childbirth condition; pregnancyRecoveryTypical = agency guidance
fieldGuide.combinedMaxWeeks: statutory cap on medical + family leave in a year; null where they are separate pools (CA, NJ) or no program
fieldGuide.weeklyMax2026: maximum weekly benefit in effect on 2026-10-09; notes give earlier 2026 figures where it changed
fieldGuide.tdiOnly: true only for HI: temporary disability insurance for pregnancy recovery, no paid bonding leave
fieldGuide.notes: reader-facing; researchNotes keeps the original research notes (source conflicts, blocked sites, method) and is not for display
fieldGuide.evidence: short verbatim quotes from the cited documents, for audit; not for display
fieldGuide.pregnancyAccommodationLaw: state law requiring reasonable accommodations for pregnancy (beyond the federal PWFA); {text, sourceIds} or {text, none: true, sourceIds: [checked]}; unverified: true when we couldn't confirm. scope: "public-only" when the law covers only government employers; "limited" when it requires less than an accommodation or break time (IN response-only, MS no extra breaks)
fieldGuide.lactationAtWorkLaw: state law on break time and/or a private space to pump at work (beyond the federal PUMP Act); same shape
fieldGuide.stateEmployeeParentalLeave: paid (or extended unpaid) parental leave for the state's own employees; same shape
fieldGuide.voluntaryPflInsuranceLaw: state law letting insurers sell family leave insurance, or a voluntary state plan; same shape
fieldGuide.civilRightsAgency: state agency that takes pregnancy-discrimination complaints from private-sector workers, or null
fieldGuide.benefitFormula: paying states only: 2026 weekly benefit rule for src/lib/pfl-calc.ts. wageInput aww|hqw (hqwDivisor 13 = rate applies to HQW/13); method marginal (each rate on its slice) | band (one rate or flat amount for the whole wage, by band) | flat; weeklyMin/Max clamp, minRule wage-if-lower; rounding cent|dollar-down|dollar-up|dollar-nearest (wageRounding and bracketRounding where the agency rounds earlier); waitingDays = unpaid days at the start of the pregnancy-recovery claim; medical = separate recovery formula (NY DBL); weeks = paid weeks after a vaginal birth / C-section and typical paid weeks before the due date; examples are agency-published (or computed: true from the published rule) and are unit-tested

fmla.text: The federal Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave in a 12-month period for a birth and to care for the newborn, or for their own serious health condition, including pregnancy complications and recovery from childbirth. Health coverage continues during leave, and you return to the same or an equivalent job.

eligibility.text: You qualify if you've worked for the employer at least 12 months and 1,250 hours in the past 12 months, at a worksite where the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles. Public agencies and schools are covered at any size.

federalPaidLeaveMandate.text: No federal law requires private employers to give paid family, maternity or parental leave. FMLA leave is unpaid, though workers can use paid leave they've earned, and the Fair Labor Standards Act doesn't require pay for time not worked.

pwfa.text: The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act requires employers with 15 or more employees to provide reasonable accommodations for limitations related to pregnancy, childbirth or related conditions unless it causes undue hardship. EEOC lists leave for health care appointments and leave to recover from childbirth as examples. It doesn't require the leave to be paid.

federalEmployeePaidParentalLeave.text: Federal civilian employees covered by title 5 FMLA can get up to 12 weeks of paid parental leave for each birth or adoption/foster placement on or after Oct. 1, 2020, used within 12 months after the birth or placement. It requires 12 months of qualifying federal service and is separate from sick and annual leave.

employerTaxCredit.text: The federal employer tax credit for paid family and medical leave (IRC section 45S) was made permanent by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, enacted July 4, 2025. It rewards employers that offer paid leave voluntarily; it doesn't give workers a right to leave.

stateCounts.text: 12 states and DC pay family and medical leave benefits now. 2 more (MD, VA) have passed laws with benefits starting in 2028, and 10 have voluntary programs or let insurers sell family leave coverage to employers. Hawaii has disability pay for pregnancy and childbirth but no paid bonding leave.

weeklyMax2026Range.text: Among paying states, the most you can get per week in 2026 ranges from $900 (DE) to $1,765 (CA) for family leave; New York's disability benefit for pregnancy recovery is capped at $170 a week.

AL.summary: Alabama has no state paid family leave program. A 2023 law lets insurers sell paid family leave policies to employers, so you're covered only if your employer buys one.
AL.programName: Voluntary paid family leave insurance (employer group policies or voluntarily purchased employee policies)
AL.wageReplacement: Set by each policy; only if your employer buys coverage (or you buy a voluntary employee policy where one is offered).
AL.waitingPeriod: Set by each policy (the law only requires the policy to say whether there is an unpaid waiting period).
AL.jobProtection: This law does not protect your job. The federal FMLA may: up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if your employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you have worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers.
AL.eligibilitySummary: Only workers covered by an employer's group disability policy that includes paid family leave, or who buy a voluntary employee policy; eligibility rules are set by the policy. No state-run program.
AL.lawCitation: Paid Family Leave Income Replacement Benefits Act, Ala. Code §§ 27-19-150 to 27-19-160; Act 2023-112 (HB 141, 2023 Regular Session), approved May 4, 2023; effective Aug. 1, 2023
AL.policyRequirements: Lets disability insurers add paid family leave benefits to employer-sponsored group policies or voluntarily purchased employee policies. Covered reasons can include caring for a family member with a serious health condition; bonding with a child in the first 12 months after birth, adoption or foster placement; FMLA military qualifying exigencies; caring for a family service member injured in the line of duty; and other reasons the policy lists. The policy must provide at least 2 weeks of benefits in a 52-consecutive-week period, and must state the benefit amount, how wages are calculated, any offsets, and any unpaid waiting period.
AL.stateLeaveLaws: No state law beyond federal FMLA was found.
AL.notes: Effective date worked out from the act: approved May 4, 2023 (Secretary of State), and Section 2 makes it effective the first day of the third month after approval, so Aug. 1, 2023. These laws only allow insurers to sell family leave insurance to employers. They do not cover your own recovery from pregnancy or childbirth, which is paid (if at all) by short-term disability insurance, and there is no state agency to apply to; claims go to the insurer named on your employer's policy. Bonding benefits must be used within 12 months of birth or placement.
AL.researchNotes:
Workplace-law fields (checked 2026-10-09): Method: queried the Alabama Legislature's own acts database (ALISON GraphQL, the same backend as alison.legislature.state.al.us) for acts matching 'lactation', 'breast', 'breastfeeding', 'express milk', 'pregnant', 'pregnancy', 'family leave' and 'parental leave'. Only workplace-relevant hits: Act 2025-81 (SB 199, state/education employee paid parental leave, effective July 1, 2025), Act 2023-112 (HB 141, PFL insurance), and Act 2022-424 (SB 31, adoption leave for certain public employers; amends §§ 16-25-11.12, 36-26-35.2, 36-26-36.2). No lactation-at-work or pregnancy accommodation act found; Act 2006-526 only covers breastfeeding in public. A Better Balance (Dec. 2025) lists Alabama among the 20 states without state pregnancy accommodation protections, and its Alabama pump guide cites only federal law. No 2025 or 2026 amendments to Ala. Code §§ 27-19-150 to -160 were found (the 'family leave' search returned only Acts 2023-112 and 2022-424). civilRightsAgency null: Alabama has no state fair-employment agency that takes private-sector pregnancy discrimination charges; the ABB guide points workers to the U.S. DOL and EEOC. Flag for lead: Act 2022-424 summary says it requires 'certain employers' to give adoptive parents leave and '12 weeks of unpaid leave' for birth; it amends public-employee statutes, so it likely concerns public employers only, but the project's AL stateLeaveLaws ('No state law beyond federal FMLA') may deserve a second look. Act 2025-81 also covers Alabama Community College System employees and local education agency (public school) employees; leave runs concurrently with FMLA.

Recheck (2026-10-09): Act 2022-424 (SB 31) checked on the Code of Alabama (alison.legislature.state.al.us): it amended Ala. Code §§ 16-25-11.12 (Teachers' Retirement System service credit for maternity leave), 36-26-35.2 and 36-26-36.2 (state-employee leave donation, where 'family leave' means maternity or adoption leave under State Personnel Board rules). These are public-employee provisions, so stateLeaveLaws ('no state law beyond federal FMLA' for private-sector workers) stands.

pregnancyAccommodationLaw.text: No state pregnancy accommodation law found as of October 2026. The federal Pregnant Workers Fairness Act covers employers with 15+ employees.

lactationAtWorkLaw.text: No state lactation-at-work law found as of October 2026. Federal PUMP Act rules apply.

stateEmployeeParentalLeave.text: Since July 1, 2025, Alabama gives state, public school and community college employees with 12 straight months on the job 8 weeks of leave at 100% of base pay after a birth, stillbirth or miscarriage (2 weeks for fathers), plus 8 weeks for adopting a child age 3 or younger. Employees must agree in writing to stay at least 8 weeks after the leave ends (Ala. Code § 36-6A-1 et seq.; Act 2025-81, SB 199).

voluntaryPflInsuranceLaw.text: Alabama's Paid Family Leave Income Replacement Benefits Act lets disability insurers add paid family leave to employer group policies or sell it as voluntary employee policies, covering reasons such as bonding in the first 12 months after a birth, adoption or foster placement. Policies must pay at least 2 weeks of benefits in a 52-week period. It took effect Aug. 1, 2023 (Ala. Code §§ 27-19-150 to 27-19-160; Act 2023-112, HB 141).

AK.summary: Alaska has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
AK.wageReplacement: No state paid family leave program.
AK.jobProtection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers. Alaska's Family Leave Act covers only state and local government employers, not private ones.
AK.stateLeaveLaws: No state law beyond federal FMLA was found. Alaska's Family Leave Act covers only state and local government employers, not private ones.
AK.notes: There's no state paid family leave program and no law for voluntary family leave insurance. Paid time off after a birth depends on your employer's own policy, short-term disability insurance if you have it, or paid sick time. Legislation: SB 10 (family leave wage replacement) has sat in Senate Labor & Commerce since Jan. 22, 2025; HB 193 (paid parental leave through unemployment insurance) passed the House but was in Senate Rules when the session ended in May 2026.

Paid time off after a birth depends on your employer's own policy, short-term disability insurance if you have it, or paid sick time. Legislation: SB 10 (family leave wage replacement) has sat in Senate Labor & Commerce since Jan. 22, 2025; HB 193 (paid parental leave through unemployment insurance) passed the House but was in Senate Rules when the session ended in May 2026.

Workplace-law fields (checked 2026-10-09): Accommodation: AS 39.20.520 (transfer) applies only to the state and political subdivisions with 21+ employees (AS 39.20.550(2)); year 1992 per A Better Balance; DOL Women's Bureau map also says protections apply only to public employees. Alaska's general anti-discrimination law (AS 18.80.220) bars pregnancy discrimination but has no accommodation duty. Lactation: DOL map marks Alaska 'no' (only federal protections) and notes the uncodified state-employee policy; AAM 280.460 (rev. 07-10) verified in the Dept. of Administration PDF. Treated as none because it is an internal personnel policy, not a statute or rule. Bills checked: full 34th Legislature HB and SB lists (2025-2026); no lactation, pregnancy accommodation or family leave insurance bill was enacted. SB 10 (paid family leave/wage replacement insurance) stayed in Senate L&C; HB 193 (UI-based paid parental leave) ended in Senate Rules. State employees: AS 39.20.305 gives 18 workweeks in 12 months for pregnancy/childbirth/adoption; accrued paid leave must be used down to 5 days, rest is leave without pay (AAM 280.360-.390 confirms AFLA administration). No governor's order or statute giving paid parental leave to state employees was found. Year of AS 39.20.305 not confirmed from a primary source, so omitted. WebSearch budget ran out mid-task; remaining checks used legislature sites directly.

pregnancyAccommodationLaw.text: Alaska's law covers only public employers: a pregnant employee of the state or a local government with 21+ employees can ask to transfer to an open, less strenuous or less hazardous job that her health care provider recommends. Private employers aren't covered by a state accommodation law (Alaska Stat. § 39.20.520, 1992).

lactationAtWorkLaw.text: No state lactation-at-work law found as of October 2026. A state payroll policy lets state employees pump as needed in a private space that isn't a bathroom (Alaska Administrative Manual 280.460).

stateEmployeeParentalLeave.text: Alaska state employees can take up to 18 weeks of family leave within 12 months for pregnancy, birth or adoption, compared with 12 weeks under FMLA. Most of it is unpaid: employees must first use accrued paid leave until 5 days remain (Alaska Stat. § 39.20.305). Local governments with 21+ employees must offer the same 18 weeks.

voluntaryPflInsuranceLaw.text: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026.

Paid time off after a birth depends on your employer's own policy, short-term disability insurance if you have it, or paid sick time. Workplace-law fields (checked 2026-10-09): State employees (unverified): no parental leave statute appears in the ARS Title 38 or Title 41 section lists (only military, donor, sick-leave payout and LWOP sections), and none of Gov. Hobbs' executive orders (2023-2026) concern parental leave. If Arizona has a state-employee paid parental leave benefit it would be an ADOA personnel rule or policy, but hr.az.gov, benefitoptions.az.gov, doa.az.gov and the Arizona Administrative Code (apps.azsos.gov, azsos.gov) all returned HTTP 403 to us, and the session's web-search budget was exhausted, so we could not check. Needs a manual check of ADOA HR policy / A.A.C. Title 2, Ch. 5.1. Pregnancy: A.R.S. 41-1463(G) requires equal treatment; ABB (Dec. 2025) lists Arizona among states without protections. Lactation: ARS Title 41 has only a public-accommodation breastfeeding section (41-1443); Title 23 has none. 2026 session laws (all chapters listed on azleg.gov) include no workplace lactation, pregnancy accommodation, state-employee parental leave or family leave insurance bill (HB 2072 is lactation care provider certification). We could not load the 2025 session-law list (the site's session switcher didn't respond to URL parameters), so 2025 relies on ABB (Dec. 2025) and Mercer (Feb. 2026).

Recheck (2026-10-09): stateEmployeeParentalLeave resolved: ADOA HR pages (hr.az.gov) return 403 to curl but load in a real browser. ADOA still lists the paid parental leave program as a pilot with no end date.

lactationAtWorkLaw.text: No state lactation-at-work law found as of October 2026. Federal PUMP Act rules apply.

stateEmployeeParentalLeave.text: Arizona gives eligible State Personnel System employees up to 12 weeks of paid parental leave after a birth, adoption or foster placement on or after Jan. 1, 2023, to use within 12 months, so they don't have to use their own leave or go unpaid. The state still calls it a pilot program (announced September 2023). State employees can also use up to 480 hours a year of their sick leave to care for a sick child, spouse or parent.

AR.summary: Arkansas has no state paid family leave program. A 2023 law lets insurers sell paid family leave policies to employers, so you're covered only if your employer buys one.
AR.wageReplacement: Set by each policy; only if your employer buys coverage.
AR.waitingPeriod: Set by each policy (the law only requires the policy to say whether there is an unpaid waiting period).
AR.jobProtection: This law does not protect your job. The federal FMLA may: up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if your employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you have worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers.
AR.eligibilitySummary: Only employees whose employer buys a family leave insurance policy or rider; eligibility rules are set by the policy. No state-run program.
AR.lawCitation: Ark. Code Ann. § 23-62-112 (Family leave insurance); Act 84 of 2023 (SB 111, 94th General Assembly), approved Feb. 17, 2023
AR.policyRequirements: Creates 'family leave insurance' as a line of insurance that accident and health or life insurers may issue to an employer to replace part of an employee's income lost due to the birth or adoption of a child, foster placement, caring for a family member with a serious health condition, or a family member's active military duty or call to duty. It can be a rider or amendment to a group disability income policy, included in that policy, or a separate group policy bought by an employer. The statute sets NO minimum number of weeks or benefit amount.
AR.stateLeaveLaws: No state law beyond federal FMLA was found.
AR.notes: Act 84 was approved Feb. 17, 2023 and has no emergency clause or stated effective date, so it took effect on Arkansas's general effective date for acts of the 2023 regular session (91 days after the session adjourned). The Vermont legislature's March 2026 chart lists Arkansas as effective in 2023. These laws only allow insurers to sell family leave insurance to employers. They do not cover your own recovery from pregnancy or childbirth, which is paid (if at all) by short-term disability insurance, and there is no state agency to apply to; claims go to the insurer named on your employer's policy.

An employer doesn't have to provide break time if it would cause undue hardship (Ark. Code § 11-5-116; Act 621 of 2009).

stateEmployeeParentalLeave.text: Arkansas state agencies can grant female state employees with 1+ year of service up to 12 consecutive weeks of maternity leave at full pay within 12 weeks of a birth, or of adopting or fostering a baby under 1, without using up sick or annual leave first (Ark. CA.summary: California pays new moms through State Disability Insurance (usually up to 4 weeks before and 6 to 8 weeks after birth), then up to 8 weeks of Paid Family Leave to bond, at 70% to 90% of wages up to $1,765 a week in 2026.
CA.programName: California State Disability Insurance (SDI): Disability Insurance (DI) and Paid Family Leave (PFL)
CA.pregnancyRecoveryTypical: EDD says pregnancy Disability Insurance usually lasts 10 to 12 weeks: up to 4 weeks before your due date and up to 6 weeks after a vaginal birth or 8 weeks after a C-section. Your doctor or midwife can certify longer if there are complications. After your last DI payment, EDD sends you a PFL New Mother claim (DE 2501FP) so you can add up to 8 weeks of bonding.
CA.wageReplacement: About 70% to 90% of the wages you earned 5 to 18 months before your claim, based on your highest-earning quarter: 90% for lower earners, and for higher earners 70% (or a flat $1,127 in one middle band, per EDD's table). $50/week minimum, $1,765/week maximum in 2026. DI and PFL use the same formula and max.
CA.waitingPeriod: 7-day unpaid waiting period for Disability Insurance (pregnancy/childbirth); no waiting period for PFL bonding.
CA.jobProtection: SDI and PFL do not protect your job; EDD says they pay benefits only. Job protection comes from other laws. California Pregnancy Disability Leave (PDL) gives up to 4 months of job-protected leave for pregnancy disability at employers with 5 or more employees, with no tenure or hours requirement. CFRA gives up to 12 weeks of job-protected bonding leave at employers with 5 or more employees if you have worked there at least 12 months and 1,250 hours. Federal FMLA covers employers with 50 or more employees within 75 miles. PDL and CFRA bonding leave are separate, so PDL runs first and CFRA bonding runs after.
CA.eligibilitySummary: You need at least $300 in wages with SDI withheld ("CASDI" on your paystub) in your base period, about 5 to 18 months before your claim. You must be employed or actively looking for work when the leave starts, and you must lose wages. For DI you must be unable to do your regular work for at least 8 days and be certified by a licensed health professional; a licensed midwife or nurse-midwife can certify normal pregnancy and postpartum. There is no minimum hours or job-tenure test. Citizenship and immigration status don't affect eligibility. Self-employed people can buy Disability Insurance Elective Coverage (DIEC). Some public employees are not covered.
CA.notes: If you are pregnant, apply for DI first (online at https://edd.ca.gov/en/disability/step-2-apply/ or by mail). File no earlier than 9 days and no later than 49 days after your disability starts. After your last DI payment, EDD sends a PFL New Mother claim (DE 2501FP) to move you onto bonding benefits. Each parent can take their own 8 weeks of PFL bonding within 12 months of the birth. There is no combined cap: DI (up to 52 weeks per disability) and PFL (8 weeks) are separate. A typical uncomplicated birth is about 10–12 weeks of DI plus 8 weeks of PFL, roughly 18–20 weeks paid. Since January 1, 2025, employers cannot require you to use vacation before PFL (AB 2123), and benefits are 70%/90% (SB 951). SB 590 adds a 'designated person' to PFL family care starting July 1, 2028; it doesn't affect bonding. San Francisco employers with 20+ employees must top up PFL bonding pay under the city's Paid Parental Leave Ordinance. EDD hadn't posted a 2027 maximum as of October 2026.

Benefit formula (checked 2026-10-09): Bands come from EDD's dollar-increment benefit table DE 2589 (Rev. 17 (1-26), claims beginning on or after Jan. 1, 2026), not the rounder thresholds on EDD's web page. The web page lists 90% up to HQW $16,279.90, then $1,127 from $16,279.91 to $20,931.30, then 70%. DE 2589 shows the flat $1,127 starting at HQW $16,264.45, and EDD rounds every amount UP to the next whole dollar (e.g. HQW $722.50 -> $51, $20,967.15 -> $1,130). Using the web-page cutoff with that rounding would give $1,128 for HQW of about $16,279-16,279.90, which DE 2589 doesn't. With the bands above (rate x HQW/13, then dollar-up, then the $50 min and $1,765 max), I checked every row of DE 2589 (all 1,716 parsed ranges, low and high ends) and got 0 mismatches. Max $1,765 is reached at HQW $32,760.01. DE 2588 (Rev. 23 (2-26)) is the 10-dollar summary version of the same table. EDD's online calculator is interactive and wasn't used. The $300 eligibility test is on total base-period wages, so HQW below $722.50 still pays the $50 minimum when total base-period wages reach $300. DI waiting period: 7 unpaid calendar days, no waiting period for PFL bonding.

Most workers get about 90% of their weekly wages, and higher earners get 70% (or a flat $1,127 in one middle band), from $50 up to $1,765 a week. CO.summary: Colorado pays up to 12 weeks for pregnancy and bonding combined (16 with a pregnancy or childbirth complication), at up to 90% of wages, max $1,448.02 a week from July 1, 2026.
CO.programName: Colorado Paid Family and Medical Leave Insurance (FAMLI)
CO.pregnancyRecoveryTypical: FAMLI says most birthing parents file a Pregnancy Leave claim first (once a health care provider certifies the need), then a separate Bonding Leave claim after the birth. Both come out of the same 12-week balance, unless your provider certifies a pregnancy or childbirth complication, which uses a separate 4-week balance (up to 16 weeks) and can continue after the baby is born.
CO.wageReplacement: 90% of your average weekly wage up to half the state average weekly wage, plus 50% of wages above that. Max $1,448.02/week from July 1, 2026 ($1,381.45 earlier in 2026).
CO.jobProtection: Yes, in the FAMLI Act itself: if you have worked for your employer at least 180 days before leave, you have the right to return to your job or an equivalent one with equivalent pay and benefits. Health insurance continues during leave, and retaliation is banned for everyone. If your local government employer opted out of FAMLI and you opted in yourself, your job is not protected by FAMLI, though federal FMLA may apply.
CO.eligibilitySummary: Most Colorado employees qualify after earning $2,500 in Colorado wages subject to FAMLI premiums in the last 5 completed calendar quarters; there is no minimum time with your current employer. Private employers and state government are covered; local governments can opt out. Self-employed and gig workers (and employees of opted-out local governments) can opt in for at least 3 years.
CO.notes: Weekly max changed mid-2026: $1,381.45 through June 30, 2026 and $1,448.02 from July 1, 2026 (based on the 2026-2027 Colorado average weekly wage of $1,608.91). FAMLI does not say whether claims that began before July 1 move to the new cap. A birthing parent with a certified pregnancy or childbirth complication can get 16 weeks in total (12 otherwise). Since Jan. 1, 2026 (SB 25-144), parents whose baby is in a NICU can also get up to 12 additional weeks of Neonatal Care Leave from a separate balance, so the total can reach 28 weeks in rare cases. Standard pregnancy leave reduces the 12 weeks left for bonding; complication and NICU leave do not. Bonding must be taken within 12 months of birth, both parents can file for bonding, and you cannot file a bonding claim before the baby is born (you can start the application up to 30 days early as a draft). Your benefit year runs 12 months from your first day of FAMLI leave. Give your employer 30 days' notice when possible. 2026 premium: 0.88% of wages up to $184,500, split 50/50 (employers with fewer than 10 employees don't pay the employer half). Employers may use an approved private plan instead.

CT.summary: Connecticut pays up to 12 weeks for pregnancy, recovery and bonding combined (14 with a serious pregnancy complication), at up to 95% of wages, max $1,016.40 a week in 2026.
CT.programName: Connecticut Paid Leave (CT Paid Family and Medical Leave Insurance Program)
CT.pregnancyRecoveryTypical: CT Paid Leave covers prenatal appointments, pregnancy complications, childbirth and the post-delivery 'recovery period' your provider certifies. It sets no standard number of weeks. Pregnancy, recovery and bonding all come out of the same 12 weeks, plus up to 2 extra weeks (14 total) if you have a serious health condition during pregnancy.
CT.wageReplacement: 95% of your average weekly wage up to 40 times the CT minimum wage ($677.60 in 2026), plus 60% of the amount above that. Capped at 60 times the minimum wage: $1,016.40/week in 2026.
CT.jobProtection: CT Paid Leave itself does not protect your job; it only replaces income. Job protection comes from the CT Family and Medical Leave Act, which covers almost all employers with 1+ employee in CT (not municipalities or the federal government). You qualify after 3 months with your employer, with no hours requirement. It gives 12 weeks plus 2 for pregnancy incapacity. Federal FMLA (50+ employees, 12 months, 1,250 hours) may also apply. You request job-protected leave from your employer separately from your CT Paid Leave claim.
CT.eligibilitySummary: You must be working for a covered CT employer now, or have worked for one in the last 12 weeks, and have earned at least $2,325 from covered employers in your highest-earning quarter of the base period (first 4 of the last 5 completed quarters). Most private employers with 1+ CT employee are covered. Self-employed people and sole proprietors can enroll. Bonding must be used within 12 months of the birth.
CT.notes: The 12 weeks is a rolling 12-month look-back from your first day of benefits, and pregnancy/childbirth leave and bonding leave share it. So a mom who uses 6 weeks for delivery recovery has 6 bonding weeks left. The 2 extra weeks apply only to a serious health condition that causes incapacity during pregnancy, not to bonding. Apply through ctpaidleave.org (CT.gov account, Aflac claims portal), ideally 30 days before leave. Bonding is block leave unless your employer approves intermittent or reduced-schedule leave. A spouse or equivalent partner can take caregiver leave during the pregnancy and recovery, and either parent can take bonding. The weekly cap rises automatically with the CT minimum wage each January 1. The 2027 cap depends on the 2027 minimum wage, which hadn't been posted as of October 2026. No 2026 benefit-level or duration changes were found.

Benefit formula (checked 2026-10-09): All three examples are CTPLA's own worked examples, which use the 2026 minimum wage of $16.94 ($677.60 threshold, $1,016.40 cap). Example 1: Q1 $2,200 + Q4 $2,400 = $4,600 / 26 = $176.92, truncated to $176, x 95% = $167.20. Example 2: AWW $701 gives $657.76. Example 3: AWW $1,346 calculates to $1,044.76, capped at $1,016.40. CTPLA truncates the AWW (two highest base-period quarters / 26) to the next lower whole dollar BEFORE applying the rates. The calculator can't express that, so I added the optional key wageRounding: 'dollar-down' (truncate the input AWW). Treat it as a no-op if unsupported, since a user typing a whole-dollar AWW gets the same result. The benefit itself is kept to the cent. Minimum-wage changes during an active claim don't change the benefit. Weeks evidence: CTPLA's 'Chris' example on the Starting or Expanding my Family page: 'After Chris gives birth via cesarean section, the healthcare provider tells Chris to take 8 weeks to recover from the birth.' Chris then uses the remaining 4 weeks for bonding. In the 'Pat' example, Pat uses 6 weeks to recover and then 6 weeks to bond. No waiting period.

DE.summary: Delaware pays 80% of wages, up to $900 a week, for up to 12 weeks to bond and up to 6 weeks of medical leave, 12 weeks combined. Benefits started January 1, 2026; you need 12 months and 1,250 hours with an employer of 10+ workers.
DE.programName: Delaware Paid Leave (Delaware Paid Family and Medical Leave Insurance Program)
DE.wageReplacement: 80% of your average weekly wages over the prior 12 months; min $100/week (or your full wage if you earn less); max $900/week in 2026 and 2027.
DE.waitingPeriod: None in the law (no unpaid waiting week). DDOL says the first payment takes about two weeks to process after approval (anti-fraud review), then payments are weekly.
DE.jobProtection: Yes, in the Paid Leave law: covered employees must be restored to the same job or one with equivalent seniority, status, pay and benefits, and health coverage continues during leave. You only qualify (and are protected) after 12 months and 1,250 hours with your current employer, and only if that employer has 10+ employees in Delaware (10-24 employees: parental leave only).
DE.eligibilitySummary: You must work primarily in Delaware, for an employer with at least 10 Delaware employees, and have worked for that employer at least 12 months and 1,250 hours (about 25 hours/week) in the last 12 months. Employers with 10-24 employees only have to provide parental (bonding) leave; 25+ employees must also provide medical, family caregiving and military leave. Part-time or short-term workers may be put on a waiver and excluded. No self-employed opt-in found in the law.
DE.notes: Claims began Jan. 1, 2026. A birthing mom gets at most 12 paid weeks in a 12-month application year, whatever the mix: up to 12 weeks of parental leave per year, plus medical leave of up to 6 weeks per 24 months (and medical leave only if your employer has 25+ employees). Pregnancy or childbirth recovery would come from that 6-week medical bank, and DDOL gives no recovery-length guidance. The tenure test is tied to your current employer, so changing jobs means a new 12-month wait before you can claim. Parental leave must be taken continuously unless your employer's policy allows otherwise, and it must be used before the child's first birthday. If both parents work for the same employer, the employer may cap the two of you at 12 weeks combined (19 Del. C. 3703(b)). Employers with fewer than 25 employees may elect, with notice, a parental-leave limit for 5 years from the start of benefits (19 Del. C. 3703(f): 'for each employee to exercise not less than half of the employee's parental leave'), so ask your employer whether it made this election. After 2027 the $900 max is CPI-adjusted. Employers may use an approved private plan. Funding: 0.8% of wages, and employers may deduct up to half from pay.
DE.researchNotes: Benefit formula (checked 2026-10-09): Example 1 comes from the Benefits Contribution Calculator embedded on DDOL's employee page (labor.delaware.gov/delaware-paid-leave/employees/, iframe degovwidgets.netlify.app/benefits-contributions-calc, form DDOLUI 40326), run 2026-10-09. Annual wages of $39,000 returned an 'Estimated Weekly Benefit' of $600.00. $58,500 and $100,000 both returned $900.00. Example 2: the DDOL FAQ's $58,500/year = $1,125 AWW, which hits the $900 max. Examples 3-4 are computed from 19 Del. C. § 3704(a)(2): AWW $110 gives 80% = $88, raised to the $100 minimum; AWW $80 gets the full $80 wage. Rounding conflict: § 3704(a)(1) says 80% of AWW 'rounded up to the nearest even $1.00 increment', which I read as rounding the benefit up to the next whole dollar ('dollar-up'). DDOL's calculator code is Math.min(0.8*annual/52, 900) shown to the cent, with no rounding and no minimum, so it estimates up to $0.99 lower than the statute. All examples are whole-dollar, so they pass under either reading. The $900 max applies in 2026 and 2027, then is CPI-indexed. No waiting period: the ~2-week first-payment delay is anti-fraud processing, and those weeks are still paid.

benefitFormula.explain: Delaware pays 80% of your average weekly wage over the past 12 months, at least $100 a week (or your full wage if you earn less than $100) and no more than $900 a week in 2026.

weeks.note: Delaware caps all leave at 12 weeks a year. Childbirth recovery comes from the medical-leave bank of 6 weeks per 24 months (only at employers with 25+ employees), so a C-section is still capped at 6 recovery weeks. DC.summary: DC pays up to 12 weeks of parental leave to bond plus 2 weeks of prenatal leave, at up to 90% of wages, max $1,100 a week for claims filed from October 1, 2026.
DC.programName: District of Columbia Paid Family Leave (Universal Paid Leave Amendment Act)
DC.pregnancyRecoveryTypical: DC gives up to 2 weeks of prenatal leave during pregnancy, in full-day increments for prenatal appointments, pregnancy treatment or doctor-ordered bed rest. After the birth you get up to 12 weeks of parental (bonding) leave, so up to 14 weeks total around the birth. Medical leave covers pregnancy complications or stillbirth, but it counts toward the same 12-week yearly cap.
DC.wageReplacement: 90% of your average weekly wage up to 150% of DC's minimum wage times 40 hours, plus 50% of the amount above that. Max $1,100/week for applications filed on or after October 1, 2026 ($1,190/week for applications filed October 1, 2025 to September 30, 2026).
DC.waitingPeriod: None (the one-week waiting period was eliminated for claims filed on or after July 25, 2022).
DC.jobProtection: DC Paid Family Leave does not protect your job, but it does prohibit retaliation, enforced by the DC Office of Human Rights. Job protection comes from the DC Family and Medical Leave Act: employers with 20+ employees, for workers employed 1 year and 1,000 hours in the past 12 months, with up to 16 weeks of family leave and 16 weeks of medical leave in 24 months. Federal FMLA may also apply. Per the official notice, workers at employers with fewer than 20 employees have no job protection when taking DC PFL.
DC.eligibilitySummary: You must be a covered employee of a private-sector DC employer, generally spending more than half your work time in DC, with wages your employer reported to DC for unemployment insurance. Coverage must be for some or all of the 52 weeks before your qualifying event, and you must be currently employed when you apply. DC government, federal government and WMATA employees are not covered (the OPFL questionnaire also lists religious institutions). Self-employed people who work more than half the time in DC can opt in. Apply within 30 days after the event; you can't apply before it happens.
DC.notes: BIG 2026 CHANGE: The FY2027 Budget Support Act of 2026 (Bill 26-661, final Council vote July 7, 2026) cut benefits for applications filed on or after October 1, 2026. Medical leave drops from 12 to 10 weeks, family caregiving from 12 to 6 weeks, and the weekly maximum from $1,190 to $1,100. Parental (bonding) leave stays 12 weeks and prenatal leave stays 2 weeks. Your application date decides which rules apply, not your leave dates, and approved claims are unchanged. OPFL says the reduced structure lasts through October 1, 2030. Medical leave is now up to 10 weeks (12 for claims filed before October 1, 2026). By statute, prenatal plus medical leave can't exceed the medical maximum. The overall cap is 12 weeks in 52 for any mix of parental, family and medical leave, plus prenatal leave on top of parental leave, for 14 total. Your partner can take their own 12 weeks of parental leave.

I used the stated $18.40 (the statute ties the bend point to the current DC minimum wage), but couldn't confirm the July 1, 2026 minimum wage on a DOES page (does.dc.gov blocked scripted access, and the web-search budget was used up). The three examples (AWW $500, $1,000, $2,000 -> $450.00, $900.00, $1,100.00) are live calculator output and come out the same under either bend point. Applications filed Sept 30, 2026 or earlier use the $1,190 max. No waiting period for claims filed on or after July 25, 2022. Cents: the calculator uses toFixed(2), and the statute has no rounding rule.

weeks.note: DC has no separate childbirth-recovery benefit. You get up to 2 weeks of prenatal leave before the birth and 12 weeks of parental leave after it (14 total). Medical leave for complications counts inside the same 12-week cap, so a C-section doesn't add paid weeks.

FL.summary: Florida has no state paid family leave program. A 2023 law lets insurers sell paid family leave policies to employers, so you're covered only if your employer buys one.
FL.wageReplacement: Set by each policy; only if your employer buys coverage.
FL.waitingPeriod: Set by each policy (the law only requires the policy to say whether there is an unpaid waiting period).
FL.jobProtection: This law does not protect your job. The federal FMLA may: up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if your employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you have worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers.
FL.eligibilitySummary: Only employees whose employer buys a paid family leave insurance policy or rider; eligibility rules are set by the policy. No state-run program.
FL.lawCitation: Fla. Stat. §§ 624.6086 and 627.445; ch. 2023-149, Laws of Florida (CS/CS/HB 721), approved May 25, 2023; effective upon becoming law (May 25, 2023)
FL.policyRequirements: Lets life insurers sell paid family leave insurance to employers as a rider or amendment to a group disability income policy, inside that policy, or as a separate group policy. Covered reasons can include caring for a family member with a serious health condition; bonding with a child in the first 12 months after birth, adoption or foster placement; FMLA military qualifying exigencies; caring for a family member injured in the line of duty in the Armed Forces; and other reasons the policy lists. The policy must offer at least 2 weeks of benefits for each covered reason in a 52-consecutive-week period, and must spell out the benefit amount, the wage definition, any waiting period and offsets. Forms are reviewed by the Office of Insurance Regulation.
FL.stateLeaveLaws: No Florida law requires employers to give maternity leave. The Florida Civil Rights Act makes it illegal for employers with 15 or more employees to fire you, refuse to hire you, or treat you worse in pay or other terms of employment because of pregnancy (Fla. Stat. §§ 760.02(7) and 760.10; pregnancy added in 2015). Complaints go to the Florida Commission on Human Relations.
FL.notes: These laws only allow insurers to sell family leave insurance to employers. They do not cover your own recovery from pregnancy or childbirth, which is paid (if at all) by short-term disability insurance, and there is no state agency to apply to; claims go to the insurer named on your employer's policy. Florida's definition of serious health condition includes a pregnancy complication that threatens the life of the mother or unborn child, but only when you are caring for a family member.
FL.researchNotes:
Workplace-law fields (checked 2026-10-09): Pregnancy: Fla. Stat. 760.10 lists pregnancy as a protected class but has no accommodation duty; FCHR's employment complaint page says it 'does not enforce the federal PWFA' and that PWFA accommodation claims are handled by the EEOC. ABB (Dec. 2025) lists Florida among states without protections. Lactation: Fla. Stat. 383.015 only protects breastfeeding in any location; the 2023 courthouse lactation-space law (SB 144, eff. 7/1/2023) is for members of the public, not a workplace break law. Florida Senate keyword lists for the 2025 and 2026 sessions showed no enacted workplace lactation or pregnancy-accommodation bill. State employees: the rule text (60L-34.00421) also requires 1 year of cumulative service within the last 7 years; part-time employees get a prorated benefit. The rule chapter has a March 18, 2026 rule-development notice to update Chapter 60L-34, but the adopted version is still the Dec. 11, 2023 rule. Bills to create broader statutory paid parental leave for state employees (SB 76 in 2025, SB 220 in 2026) died in committee. Voluntary PFL: no 2025-2026 amendments to 624.6086 or 627.445 (history notes show only ch. 2023-149).

Recheck (2026-10-09): stateLeaveLaws now records the Florida Civil Rights Act's pregnancy coverage (ch. 2015-68), read on the Florida Legislature's site. It's an anti-discrimination law, not a leave mandate; the text says so. State-employee leave (Rule 60L-34.00421) was already recorded.

GA.summary: Georgia has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
GA.wageReplacement: No state paid family leave program.
GA.jobProtection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers.
GA.stateLeaveLaws: No Georgia law requires employers to give maternity leave. Georgia's Family Care Act lets employees who work 30 or more hours a week, at employers with 25 or more employees (including state and local government) that provide paid sick leave, use up to 5 days a year of earned sick leave to care for an immediate family member such as a child. It doesn't require employers to offer sick leave, and employers with an employee stock ownership plan are exempt (O.C.G.A. § 34-1-10, 2017; made permanent by Act 90 of 2023).
GA.notes: There's no state paid family leave program and no law for voluntary family leave insurance. Paid time off after a birth depends on your employer's own policy, short-term disability insurance if you have it, or paid sick time.
GA.researchNotes:
No state paid family leave program and no voluntary family leave insurance law, per NCSL (Nov 2025), Mercer (Feb 2026), NPWF (Apr 2026) and Tilt (Jul 2026). Paid time off after a birth depends on your employer's own policy, short-term disability insurance if you have it, or paid sick time. We did not re-check this state's 2026 session bill by bill, so a voluntary insurance law passed after spring 2026 can't be fully ruled out.

Workplace-law fields (checked 2026-10-09): Civil rights agency null: the Georgia Commission on Equal Opportunity (gceo.georgia.gov) enforces the Fair Employment Practices Act only against state agencies ('unlawful for a state agency to discriminate'); Georgia has no agency that takes private-employer pregnancy discrimination charges, so those go to the EEOC. Lactation: the official O.C.G.A. (Lexis) and Justia were not machine-readable/blocked, and legis.ga.gov's API requires a generated token, so we read the statute on FindLaw (marked current as of March 28, 2024) via WebFetch; quotes are verbatim from that page. FindLaw text: 'employer' means any person or entity that employs one or more employees, and 'shall not include the state and its political subdivisions'; employers with fewer than 50 employees are not subject to requirements that impose undue hardship. NCSL (June 2026) confirms Georgia requires paid lactation break time. The law states no time limit after birth. We could not verify the year of the paid-break amendment or rule out a 2025-2026 amendment bill by bill (GA API gated). State employees: SPB Rule 478-1-.16 sec. (26), revised 08/28/2026, cites O.C.G.A. 45-20-17 (paid parental leave) and 45-20-23 (maternal birth leave); we could not open those statutes or confirm their enactment years. 'Full-time' = at least 30 hours a week (O.C.G.A. 45-18-1 per the rule); the rule applies to the executive branch excluding the Board of Regents. Pregnancy: ABB (Dec. 2025) lists Georgia among states without protections; SPB Rule 478-1-.03 bars pregnancy discrimination for state employees but has no pregnancy accommodation clause. Voluntary PFL: Mercer (Feb. 2026) lists 8 insurance-law states (not GA); Tilt (Jul. 2026) says only Louisiana joined in 2026.

Recheck (2026-10-09): stateLeaveLaws now records the Family Care Act (SB 201, 2017; sunset repealed by SB 61, Act 90, signed and effective May 1, 2023), confirmed on legis.ga.gov. HB 146 (Act 225, 2021) confirmed to cover full-time local board of education employees; hours for school staff aren't stated because 2026 changes to state-employee hours may also apply to them. No state pregnancy accommodation law or voluntary PFL insurance law found.

pregnancyAccommodationLaw.text: No state pregnancy accommodation law found as of October 2026. Federal PWFA rules apply.

lactationAtWorkLaw.text: Georgia requires employers with one or more employees to give reasonable break time to pump at work, paid at the employee's regular rate, and a private place other than a restroom. Employers with fewer than 50 employees are excused where this would cause undue hardship, and state and local government employers aren't covered by this law (O.C.G.A. § 34-1-6).

stateEmployeeParentalLeave.text: Georgia gives full-time executive-branch state employees up to 240 hours (6 weeks at 40 hours a week) of paid parental leave in a 12-month period for a birth, adoption or foster placement. Employees who give birth also get up to 120 hours (3 weeks) of paid maternal birth leave in the 3 weeks after delivery. Salaried staff qualify after 6 months on the job and hourly staff after 700 hours in 6 months (O.C.G.A. §§ 45-20-17 and 45-20-23; State Personnel Board Rule 478-1-.16, revised Aug. 2026). The same paid parental leave law also covers full-time public school employees through their local boards of education (O.C.G.A. § 45-20-17, Act 225 of 2021).

HI.summary: Hawaii has no paid leave to bond, but Temporary Disability Insurance pays 58% of wages (max $871 a week in 2026) for up to 26 weeks while you recover from pregnancy and childbirth.
HI.programName: Hawaii Temporary Disability Insurance (TDI): employer-provided disability pay for off-the-job illness or injury, including pregnancy and childbirth. Hawaii has no state paid family or bonding leave.
HI.wageReplacement: TDI only (statutory plan): 58% of your average weekly wage, rounded up to the next dollar, max $871/week in 2026, for up to 26 weeks while a doctor certifies you can't work, including pregnancy and childbirth recovery. Approved employer plans may pay differently. No paid bonding leave.
HI.waitingPeriod: 7 consecutive days for TDI under a statutory plan (benefits start on the 8th day of disability); approved employer plans may differ
HI.jobProtection: TDI itself does not protect your job. The Hawaii Family Leave Law (HRS ch. 398) gives up to 4 weeks a year of job-protected family leave, including for the birth of a child, if your employer has 100+ employees in Hawaii and you've worked there 6 consecutive months. That leave is unpaid unless you use accrued leave, and you can use up to 10 days of accrued sick leave for it. Federal FMLA (50+ employees, 12 months/1,250 hours) may also apply.
HI.eligibilitySummary: To get TDI you must have at least 14 weeks of Hawaii employment in which you were paid for 20+ hours, have earned at least $400 in the 52 weeks before the disability, and be in current employment (or have left work no more than 2 weeks before the disability began). Your disability, including pregnancy, must be certified by a provider. Employers must provide the coverage; some workers (e.g., federal employees, commission-only real estate and insurance agents) are excluded.
HI.stateLeaveLaws: Hawaii's Family Leave Law gives up to 4 weeks a year of unpaid, job-protected leave, including for the birth of a child, if your employer has 100+ employees in Hawaii and you've worked there 6 consecutive months. You can use up to 10 days of accrued sick leave during it.
HI.notes: Hawaii is TDI-only: pregnancy and childbirth recovery are covered as a disability, but there is no paid leave to bond with a baby or care for family. TDI is not a state-run fund: employers buy it from an authorized insurer, self-insure, or provide equal or better sick leave under a bargaining agreement. There's no online application. Ask your employer for Form TDI-45 (DLIR says it isn't available online), have your provider certify Part C, and file within 90 days of the disability starting; claims more than 26 weeks late get nothing. Employees can be charged up to half the premium, capped at 0.5% of weekly wages ($7.50/week in 2026). Hawaii's TDI law was enacted in 1969. Some sources say the 7-day wait is shorter if you're hospitalized; DLIR's own pages state only the 7-day rule. DLIR gives no typical pregnancy-recovery length. The 26 weeks is the statutory maximum per benefit year for any covered disability.

KY.policyRequirements: Paid family leave insurance can be included in, or added as a rider to, an employer's group disability income policy, or sold as a stand-alone group policy bought by an employer. It may cover caring for a family member with a serious health condition; bonding with a child in the first 12 months after birth, adoption or foster placement; FMLA military qualifying exigencies; caring for a family member in the Armed Forces or a first responder injured in the line of duty; and other non-disability reasons in the policy. The policy must provide at least 2 weeks of benefits for each covered reason in a 52-consecutive-week period, and must state the benefit amount, the wage calculation, any unpaid waiting period, offsets and exclusions.

KY.notes: These laws only allow insurers to sell family leave insurance to employers. They do not cover your own recovery from pregnancy or childbirth, which is paid (if at all) by short-term disability insurance, and there is no state agency to apply to; claims go to the insurer named on your employer's policy.

pregnancyAccommodationLaw.text: Kentucky's Pregnant Workers Act (2019) requires employers with 15+ employees in the state to make reasonable accommodations for pregnancy, childbirth and related conditions unless it causes undue hardship. Examples in the law include more frequent or longer breaks, time off to recover from childbirth, seating, light duty, a temporary transfer and a modified schedule (KRS 344.030, 344.040).

lactationAtWorkLaw.text: Kentucky's Pregnant Workers Act counts lactation as a pregnancy-related condition, so employers with 15+ employees must provide reasonable accommodations such as extra breaks and a private space that isn't a bathroom to pump, unless it causes undue hardship (KRS 344.030, 344.040; 2019). Federal PUMP Act rules also apply.

stateEmployeeParentalLeave.text: Kentucky's personnel rules give full-time state employees in the classified and unclassified services up to 6 weeks of continuous employer-paid leave for a birth and newborn care within a year, an adoption or foster placement, or their own serious health condition, available from the first day on the job. The 6 weeks are one shared allotment that renews after 10 and 20 years of service (101 KAR 2:102 and 101 KAR 3:015, current versions effective Sept. 30, 2025).

voluntaryPflInsuranceLaw.text: Kentucky's Paid Family Leave Insurance Act lets insurers sell paid family leave coverage to employers as part of, or a rider to, a group disability policy, or as a stand-alone group policy. Covered reasons can include bonding in the first 12 months after a birth, adoption or foster placement, and policies must pay at least 2 weeks for each covered reason in a 52-week period (KRS 304.53-010 to 304.53-070; HB 179, effective April 5, 2024).

LA.summary: Louisiana has no state paid family leave program. A 2026 law lets insurers sell paid family leave policies to employers, so you're covered only if your employer buys one.
LA.wageReplacement: Set by each policy; only if your employer buys coverage.
LA.waitingPeriod: Set by each policy (the policy may set an unpaid waiting period).
LA.jobProtection: This law does not protect your job. The federal FMLA may: up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if your employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you have worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. Louisiana requires employers with more than 25 workers to allow pregnancy leave: 6 weeks for a normal pregnancy and childbirth, or the time you are disabled by pregnancy or childbirth, up to 4 months. The law does not require pay, but you may use accrued annual leave. Your employer may require reasonable notice.
LA.eligibilitySummary: Only employees whose employer buys a paid family leave insurance policy or rider; eligibility rules are set by the policy. No state-run program.
LA.lawCitation: Paid Family Leave Insurance Act, La. R.S. 22:1192.1-1192.4; Act No. 817 of the 2026 Regular Session (HB 591, Rep. Kyle M. Green Jr.), signed June 8, 2026
LA.policyRequirements: Lets licensed life or disability income insurers sell paid family leave insurance as a stand-alone policy or a rider. Covered reasons: birth, adoption or foster placement; caring for a family member with a serious health condition; military exigencies; caring for an injured service member; other leave the policy lists. Benefits must last at least 2 weeks in a 52-week period, and the policy may set an unpaid waiting period. It does not provide job protection and has no state-run program.
LA.stateLeaveLaws: Louisiana requires employers with more than 25 workers to allow pregnancy leave: 6 weeks for a normal pregnancy and childbirth, or the time you are disabled by pregnancy or childbirth, up to 4 months. The law does not require pay, but you may use accrued annual leave. Your employer may require reasonable notice.
LA.notes: New in 2026: signed June 8, 2026, after passing 95-0 and 36-0. These laws only allow insurers to sell family leave insurance to employers. They do not cover your own recovery from pregnancy or childbirth, which is paid (if at all) by short-term disability insurance, and there is no state agency to apply to.

ME.summary: Maine pays up to 12 weeks a year for pregnancy recovery and bonding combined, at up to 90% of wages, max $1,249.12 a week from July 1, 2026. Benefits started May 1, 2026.
ME.programName: Maine Paid Family and Medical Leave (PFML)
ME.wageReplacement: 90% of your average weekly wage up to half the state average weekly wage, plus 66% of wages above that, capped at the state average weekly wage: $1,249.12/week from July 1, 2026 (Maine DOL rounds it to $1,250); $1,198.84 for May-June 2026.
ME.waitingPeriod: 7 calendar days for medical leave, once per benefit year (you can use PTO during it); none for bonding and other family leave
ME.jobProtection: Yes, in the PFML law: if you've worked for your employer at least 120 consecutive days, you must be restored to your job or an equivalent one with equivalent pay, benefits and conditions. Under 120 days, your employer may restore you but doesn't have to. Retaliation is banned for everyone. PFML runs at the same time as federal FMLA and Maine family medical leave when they apply.
ME.eligibilitySummary: You must have earned at least 6 times the state average weekly wage (about $7,190 at the 2025-26 rate, about $7,495 at the July 2026 rate) in Maine during your base period, the first 4 of the last 5 completed calendar quarters. Covers almost everyone employed in Maine, whatever the employer's size. Self-employed people can opt in. Federal employees aren't covered, and Tribal government employees aren't unless the Tribe opts in.
ME.notes: Benefits began May 1, 2026 (premiums since Jan. 1, 2025). The state plan is administered by Aflac (apply online or by phone); employers may use an approved private plan instead. Weekly max changed mid-2026. It equals the state average weekly wage: $1,198.84 for July 2025 to June 2026 and $1,249.12 from July 1, 2026. MDOL's June 2026 benefit chart caps benefits at 'the current average of $1,250.00 (rounded)'. MDOL doesn't say whether claims that began before July 1 get the higher cap, and 26 M.R.S. 850-C(3) also lets the department adjust the max each Jan. 1 for fund solvency. Leave cap: 12 weeks total of family + medical leave per benefit year, so pregnancy medical leave and bonding share the same 12 weeks. The law lets medical leave for pregnancy or childbirth recovery be followed right away by bonding leave, and the rule says the combined total still can't exceed 12 weeks. FMLA or Maine FMLA leave you took in the prior 12 months that didn't run at the same time reduces your PFML weeks (leave taken before May 1, 2026 doesn't count). Bonding must be within 12 months of birth. Apply up to 60 days before and no later than 90 days after leave starts, and give your employer written notice (30 days is reasonable when foreseeable). Your employer can ask to reschedule leave for 'undue hardship' within 10 business days, and you can appeal.

Benefit formula (checked 2026-10-09): CAN'T BE FULLY EXPRESSED with one end-of-calculation rounding. 12-702 CMR ch. 1 § VIII.A.2 sets the Tier 1 cap at ceil(50% x SAWW) = ceil($624.56) = $625, rounds Tier 1 (90%) up to a whole dollar, rounds Tier 2 (66%) up to a whole dollar, then adds them. I added the optional key bracketRounding: 'dollar-up' (round each bracket's product up before summing). Without it, results above $625 can come out $1 low: AWW $961.54 gives $785 instead of MDOL's $786. AWW = base-period wages / 52 (§ VIII.A.3), using the SAWW published the July 1 before the application or leave start. Examples 2-4 are rows of MDOL's 'Estimated PFML Premium and Benefit Amounts' chart: $10,000 -> $174, $50,000 -> $786, $100,000 -> $1,250 (inputs are annual / 52, to the cent). I checked other rows ($35k -> $595, $40k -> $659, $85k -> $1,230) and they match the per-tier rule with a $625 cap. MAX DOUBT: by statute (26 M.R.S. § 850-C(3)) the cap is the SAWW, $1,249.12. MDOL's chart caps at '$1,250.00 (rounded)'. With clamp-then-dollar-up, a $1,249.12 cap displays as $1,250, which matches the chart, so example 4 expects $1,250. Aflac might actually pay $1,249.12 at the cap. Example 1 is from MDOL's March 2026 webinar ('90% of $300 = $270'). That slide used the older $1,198 SAWW, but $300 is under both Tier 1 caps, so the result is the same under 2026 rules. The webinar's other examples ($867, the $1,198 cap) use the old SAWW and were skipped. Waiting period: 7 calendar days at the start of medical leave, once per benefit year, unpaid (accrued PTO can cover it). It doesn't apply to family (bonding) leave.

MD.summary: Maryland passed paid family and medical leave, but benefits don't start until January 2028: up to 12 weeks (24 with both recovery and bonding) at up to 90% of wages, max $1,000 a week.
MD.programName: Maryland Family and Medical Leave Insurance (FAMLI)
MD.wageReplacement: When benefits start in January 2028: 90% of your average weekly wage up to 65% of the state average weekly wage, plus 50% of wages above that; min $50, max $1,000/week through Dec. 31, 2028, CPI-adjusted after that. No benefits are paid in 2026.
MD.waitingPeriod: None (benefits from the first day of leave)
MD.jobProtection: Yes, in the FAMLI law: when leave ends, your employer must restore you to an equivalent position, and during leave can fire you only for cause. The only exception is if denying restoration is needed to prevent 'substantial and grievous economic injury' to the employer, the employer gives notice, and you then choose not to return. There is no separate job-tenure test beyond FAMLI's 680-hour eligibility rule. FAMLI runs at the same time as federal FMLA when both apply.
MD.eligibilitySummary: Once benefits start, you'll need to have worked at least 680 hours in a Maryland-based job in the 4 reported calendar quarters before you apply or your leave begins (hours can come from more than one employer). There is no minimum earnings test. Covers employees of employers of any size; employers with fewer than 15 employees don't pay the employer share. Federal employees aren't covered. Self-employed Marylanders will be able to opt in later.
MD.notes: Payroll contributions start Jan. 1, 2027 (first payment due April 30, 2027) and benefits start January 2028 (the FAMLI homepage says 'Starting January 1, 2028'). Md. Code, Lab. & Empl. 8.3-701(a)(1), as amended by 2025 HB 102 (Ch. 363), lets claims begin on a date the Secretary announces, between Jan. 1, 2027 and Jan. 3, 2028. Some older sources give July 2027 and July 2028 dates, from a 2025 bill (SB 355) that didn't pass. No 2026 bill changed the timeline: the 2026 session's only FAMLI-related bill (HB 1579, about state personnel) was withdrawn, and the 2026 budget act (Ch. 6) has no FAMLI provisions. Maryland Labor's homepage says benefits start January 1, 2028; other pages say only 'January 2028'. The claims website is still being built, so there's no apply link yet. Parents of babies born in 2027 can take bonding leave after benefits start, as long as it's within the child's first year. Spouses can both take FAMLI at the same time, even at the same employer. Up to 12 weeks per benefit year, plus an extra 12 (24 total) if you have both your own serious health condition (e.g., pregnancy/childbirth recovery) and bonding in the same year. Contributions are 0.9% of wages up to the Social Security wage base, and employers may withhold up to half. Employers may use an approved private plan.

MA.summary: Massachusetts pays up to 20 weeks of medical leave for pregnancy and recovery plus 12 weeks to bond, capped at 26 weeks a year, at up to 80% of wages, max $1,230.39 a week in 2026.
MA.programName: Massachusetts Paid Family and Medical Leave (PFML)
MA.pregnancyRecoveryTypical: DFML sets no standard number of weeks: your health care provider decides how much medical leave you need for pregnancy complications and recovery after childbirth (up to 20 weeks). DFML's examples include 6 weeks of prenatal bed rest plus 8 weeks of recovery, or 10 weeks of recovery after birth. You can then add up to 12 weeks of bonding, within a 26-week yearly cap.
MA.wageReplacement: 80% of your individual average weekly wage up to half the state average weekly wage ($1,922.48 in 2026), plus 50% of the amount above that. Max $1,230.39/week for benefit years starting in 2026 (64% of the state average); $1,284.61 in 2027. Your rate is set for your whole 52-week benefit year.
MA.waitingPeriod: 7 calendar days, unpaid, counted against your leave. It's waived when bonding leave immediately follows medical leave for pregnancy or childbirth recovery, so add bonding to the same application.
MA.jobProtection: Yes, the PFML law itself protects your job. When you return, your employer must restore you to the same or an equivalent position with the same status, pay, benefits, length-of-service credit and seniority, and must keep your health insurance during leave. The law has no tenure or employer-size test for covered employees. Exceptions: layoffs of comparable coworkers, or a term or project job that ended. Any negative change during leave or within 6 months after is presumed retaliation. This applies even if your employer uses a private plan. The Massachusetts Parental Leave Act may also apply.
MA.eligibilitySummary: Most Massachusetts employees are covered. You must have earned at least the DUA minimum ($6,300 currently) in the last 4 completed calendar quarters, and at least 30 times your weekly benefit amount. Self-employed people can opt in through MassTaxConnect, for at least 3 years. Municipal employees are covered only if their employer opts in. If your employer has an approved private plan, you apply through that plan instead of DFML.
MA.notes: Apply up to 60 days before your leave (online at paidleave.mass.gov). Give your employer 30 days' notice when possible. If pregnant, apply for medical leave first. Your application stays pending until you confirm your delivery date. Then add bonding to the same application to avoid a second 7-day waiting period. Both parents can each take 12 weeks of bonding within the child's first year, at the same time or at different times. Changes: the 2027 max ($1,284.61) applies to benefit years starting in 2027, while a leave inside a 2026 benefit year keeps the 2026 rate.

MI.summary: Michigan has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
MI.wageReplacement: No state paid family leave program.
MI.jobProtection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers. Michigan's civil rights law only requires employers to treat pregnancy and childbirth like other conditions affecting ability to work, including under their leave policies.
MI.stateLeaveLaws: No state law beyond federal FMLA was found. Michigan's civil rights law only requires employers to treat pregnancy and childbirth like other conditions affecting ability to work, including under their leave policies.
MI.notes: There's no state paid family leave program and no law for voluntary family leave insurance. Paid time off after a birth depends on your employer's own policy, short-term disability insurance if you have it, or paid sick time. MN.summary: Minnesota pays up to 12 weeks of pregnancy-related medical leave and 12 weeks to bond, 20 weeks combined, at up to 90% of wages, max $1,423 a week in 2026. Benefits started January 1, 2026.
MN.programName: Minnesota Paid Leave (Paid Family and Medical Leave)
MN.pregnancyRecoveryTypical: Up to 12 weeks of Pregnancy-related Medical Leave, as long as your provider certifies; DEED's examples use 6 weeks of recovery after birth, or 8 weeks after a C-section, followed by 12 weeks of Bonding Leave (up to 20 weeks total). Take the medical leave first, then bonding.
MN.wageReplacement: 90% of wages up to half the state average weekly wage, 66% of wages between half and 100% of it, and 55% of wages above it; max $1,423/week (the state average weekly wage) in 2026.
MN.waitingPeriod: None (but except for bonding, a claim must be based on a single qualifying event lasting at least 7 calendar days)
MN.jobProtection: Yes, in the Paid Leave law: you must be restored to your job or an equivalent position. Job protection generally starts 90 days after your date of hire, but DEED says Pregnancy-related Medical Leave and Bonding Leave are protected no matter how long you've worked there. Retaliation is banned from day one. Federal FMLA, Minnesota's Pregnancy and Parental Leave Act and Earned Sick and Safe Time may add protections and may run at the same time.
MN.eligibilitySummary: You must have earned at least 5.3% of the state's average annual wage in the past year (about $3,900 right now), from one or more Minnesota jobs. Covers nearly all Minnesota workers, including full-time, part-time, temporary and most seasonal workers, at employers of any size. Self-employed people, independent contractors and Tribal Nations can opt in. Federal, postal and railroad workers can't; designated seasonal hospitality jobs are excluded.
MN.notes: Minnesota Paid Leave started Jan. 1, 2026. Birthing parents need two applications: Pregnancy-related Medical Leave first, then Bonding Leave after medical leave ends. Taking bonding first can cost you the medical weeks if your provider says you've recovered. Each type is capped at 12 weeks, and the total of all types is 20 weeks in a benefit year that starts on the first day of any leave. Bonding must end before the child's first birthday (or 1 year after the baby comes home if hospitalized longer than the parent). Apply up to 60 days before leave starts. DEED's pages still say the max is 'currently $1,423' as of Oct. 9, 2026. Under Minn. Stat. 268B.04 subd. 3(e), a new max (the updated state average weekly wage) applies to leaves established on or after the last Sunday in October (Oct. 25, 2026); no new figure had been announced as of Oct. 9, 2026. Your weekly amount is fixed once your leave is established. Employers can't make you use PTO first. Employers may have an approved equivalent (private) plan. The premium is 0.88% of wages for 2026 and stays the same for 2027.

Benefit formula (checked 2026-10-09): Brackets and max are from DEED's payments page and Minn. Stat. 268B.04 subd. 3. MN defines the average weekly wage as high-quarter wages divided by 13 (DEED's calculator code: calculateAAWW = maxWage / 13.0), so an AWW input equals HQW/13. Examples are DEED calculator output: I ran the page's own inline calculation code (SAWW const 1423) with HQW = AWW x 13 (6,500; 13,000; 15,600; 26,000). The calculator truncates each bracket slice to the cent (Math.floor(x*100)/100); the example inputs give exact cents, so 'cent' rounding reproduces them. The statute is silent on rounding. No minimum weekly benefit; eligibility needs about $3,900 in base-period wages. No waiting week: except for bonding, a claim must cover a qualifying event of at least 7 calendar days. CAUTION: under 268B.04 subd. 3(e) the max resets for leaves established on or after the last Sunday in October (2026-10-25). DEED had not posted the new figure on 2026-10-09 (the page still says 'currently $1,423'), so recheck after Oct 25. The half-SAWW threshold moves with it.

evidence.quote: Paid Leave launched on January 1, 2026, and provides:
If you are a birthing parent, you may be able to take both Pregnancy-related Medical Leave and Bonding Leave. If you need both types of leave in one year, you can take up to 20 total weeks of leave.
How much time can I take? Up to 12 weeks, depending on what your healthcare provider says you need Up to 12 weeks, you choose how much time to take
If you are not a birthing parent, you may still be able to take up to 12 weeks of Bonding Leave.
For example, your medical provider might certify that you need 8 weeks to recover from birth after a Caesarean section.
The most anyone can get is the average weekly wage in Minnesota, currently $1,423 per week.
The state's maximum weekly benefit amount, computed in accordance with section 268.035, subdivision 23, applies to leaves established effective on or after the last Sunday in October.

(1) 90 percent of wages that do not exceed 50 percent of the state's average weekly wage; plus (2) 66 percent of wages that exceed 50 percent of the state's average weekly wage but not 100 percent; plus (3) 55 percent of wages that exceed 100 percent of the state's average weekly wage.
Except for a claim for benefits for bonding leave, any claim for benefits must be based on a single qualifying event of at least seven calendar days.
Job protections start 90 days after your date of hire. If you are taking Pregnancy-related Medical Leave or Bonding Leave, your job is protected no matter how long it has been since you were hired.
To receive payments, you must have earned at least $3,900 in the last year.
For weekly wages between $0 and $711.50 (half of the current state average), you get paid 90%.
For weekly wages between $711.50 and $1,423 (the current state average), you get paid 66%.
Weekly payments cannot exceed the state average weekly wage, $1,423.

benefitFormula.explain: Minnesota pays 90% of your weekly wage up to $711.50, plus 66% of the part between $711.50 and $1,423, plus 55% of anything above $1,423. The most anyone gets is $1,423 a week.

weeks.note: Pregnancy-related Medical Leave (up to 12 weeks, as your provider certifies) and Bonding Leave (up to 12 weeks) share a 20-week cap per benefit year; DEED's own examples use 6 weeks of recovery after birth or 8 after a C-section, then 12 weeks of bonding.

Paid time off after a birth depends on your employer's own policy, short-term disability insurance if you have it, or paid sick time. We did not re-check this state's 2026 session bill by bill, so a voluntary insurance law passed after spring 2026 can't be fully ruled out.

Workplace-law fields (checked 2026-10-09): Pregnancy accommodation: NRS 613.4353-613.4383 (added 2017); employer = 15+ employees (NRS 613.310); 613.4359 includes lactation; 613.438(1)(e) bars requiring leave when an accommodation is available; complaints go to NERC (NRS 613.405). Lactation: NRS 608.0193 (added 2017) for employers generally, with construction-contractor jobsite exception; NRS 281.755 (added 2017, amended 2019) for public bodies (excludes Dept. of Corrections). State employees: NRS 284.356 added 2023; also covers serious illness, family care and military deployment; leave may be split over 12 months; HR page hr.nv.gov/Resources/Publications/HR123/Attendance/PFL/ cites it. Voluntary PFL: full-text search of all 83rd (2025) session bills for "family leave insurance" hit only AB 191 (collective bargaining), not an insurer-model bill; 83rd session adjourned June 3, 2025, and the next regular session is 2027 (36th special session 2025 is the latest listed). Civil rights URL: detr.nv.gov returns an Akamai 403 to every automated client (curl, WebFetch, headless Chrome), so this page could NOT be load-verified; please spot-check it in a browser. NERC's role in taking these complaints is verified in NRS 613.405.

The female employee who is pregnant must be allowed to use the leave before and after childbirth, miscarriage or other natural resolution of her pregnancy

Restructuring a position or providing a modified work schedule.
