pregnancyAccommodationLaw.text: Nevada requires employers with 15 or more employees to provide reasonable accommodations for conditions related to pregnancy, childbirth or related medical conditions, including lactation, unless it causes undue hardship. The employer must work out the accommodation with you in a timely, good-faith process and can't force leave if an accommodation would let you keep working (Nevada Pregnant Workers' Fairness Act, NRS 613.4353 to 613.4383, 2017).

lactationAtWorkLaw.text: Nevada requires employers to give employees with a child under 1 reasonable break time, paid or unpaid, to pump, plus a private place that isn't a bathroom. Employers with fewer than 50 workers are exempt if it would cause undue hardship, and a parallel law covers public employers (NRS 608.0193 and 281.755, 2017).

stateEmployeeParentalLeave.text: Nevada gives executive-branch state employees with 12 straight months of service 8 weeks of paid family leave at 50% of regular pay, which can be used to bond with a newborn or newly adopted child. Employees must have at least 40 hours of sick leave and use any sick leave above 40 hours first (NRS 284.356, 2023).

voluntaryPflInsuranceLaw.text: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026.

NH.summary: New Hampshire has no required paid leave. You're paid only if your employer buys the Granite State plan or you buy an individual plan well ahead of time (60% of wages for 6 weeks, after a 7-month wait).
NH.programName: Granite State Paid Family Leave Plan (New Hampshire Paid Family and Medical Leave, NH PFML), insured by MetLife
NH.wageReplacement: 60% of your average weekly wage (based on the last four completed calendar quarters), with wages capped at the Social Security wage base ($184,500 in 2026); max $2,128.85/week in 2026. Only if you are enrolled: through an employer that buys the plan, or by buying an individual plan yourself.
NH.waitingPeriod: Employer plans: a one-time 7-day unpaid waiting period each benefit year. Individual plan: a one-time 7-month waiting period after enrollment before benefits are available, plus a one-week elimination period.
NH.jobProtection: NH PFML pays benefits only; it does not protect your job (MetLife). Separate laws may: federal FMLA (50+ employees, 12 months/1,250 hours, 12 weeks unpaid); NH RSA 354-A:7 VI (employers with 6+ employees must allow unpaid leave for the period you are physically disabled by pregnancy or childbirth, then return you to your job or a comparable one unless business necessity prevents it); and, from Jan. 1, 2026, RSA 275:37-f (employers with 20+ employees must allow up to 25 hours of unpaid leave in the child's first year for childbirth, postpartum and pediatric appointments, with your job held).
NH.eligibilitySummary: Voluntary. State employees are covered automatically. Any employer with a physical NH location may buy group coverage (6 or 12 weeks). If your employer offers NH PFML and you decline it, you cannot buy individual coverage. If your employer does not offer NH PFML or an equivalent plan, you can buy an individual plan (up to 6 weeks; premium capped at $5/week) during the state's 60-day annual open enrollment. You must work for an employer with an NH location (remote workers count); gig workers, contractors and people who are not employed are not eligible.
NH.stateLeaveLaws: Employers with 6+ employees must let you take leave while you're physically unable to work because of pregnancy, childbirth or a related condition, then give you back your job or a comparable one unless business necessity makes that impossible or unreasonable (RSA 354-A:7 VI). Since Jan. 1, 2026, employers with 20+ employees must also allow up to 25 hours of unpaid leave in your baby's first year for your childbirth and postpartum appointments and the baby's pediatric visits, with your job held (RSA 275:37-f). Neither law requires pay.
NH.notes: Plan ahead: the individual plan has a 7-month waiting period after enrollment and only a 60-day annual enrollment window, so you have to enroll well before your due date. Weeks: 6 for individual-plan members and for the statutory default; employer plans can offer 6 or 12 weeks. Bonding, your own pregnancy or childbirth recovery, and family care all come out of the same pool per benefit year. Benefits for your own health condition (including pregnancy) are paid only if you don't qualify for insured short-term disability or workers' comp. Employers buying through MetLife can get a 50% Business Enterprise Tax credit for 6 weeks of coverage. Sources differ on job protection: one benefits consultancy says employers with 50+ employees must protect the job of an employee who opts in, but MetLife says NH PFML gives no job protection, and we found no such provision in the state law. Benefits start date: RSA 21-I:111 required coverage to be in place and available by Jan. 1, 2023. Individual buyers could not be paid before about Aug. 2023 because of the 7-month wait. Check paidfamilymedicalleave.nh.gov for 2027 individual enrollment dates. MetLife says individual plans most often take effect Jan. 1 or Feb. 1. Legislation: HB 1761 (2026), which would have created a publicly run program, was sent to interim study on Feb. 19, 2026. No mandatory program has been enacted. The 2027 cap will follow the 2027 Social Security wage base (not yet published by MetLife).

Workplace-law fields (checked 2026-10-09): Pregnancy accommodation: RSA 354-A:7 VI(c) only requires pregnancy to be treated like any other temporary disability (comparative), and VI(b) requires disability leave plus reinstatement; neither is a general accommodation mandate. A Better Balance (Dec. 2025) lists New Hampshire among the 20 states without state protections; earlier accommodation bills (SB 68 of 2021-2022) died in interim study. Lactation: RSA 275:78-83 enacted by 2023 c. 191:20 (HB 358, part of the 'MOMnibus'), effective July 1, 2025; the civil penalty (RSA 275:82) took effect July 1, 2026. 'Expression of milk' excludes breastfeeding. State employees: RSA 21-I:102 II requires coverage for FMLA-type reasons except the employee's own health condition; MetLife's state-employee plan may cover more, but the state PFML site (paidfamilymedicalleave.nh.gov) and das.nh.gov returned 403 to automated requests, so we could not check the plan terms. Mercer (Feb. 2026) confirms the program 'requires PFL benefits for state employees'. Civil rights agency: name and complaint role confirmed from RSA 354-A (State Commission for Human Rights; RSA 354-A:21 complaint procedure). Both www.humanrights.nh.gov and www.nh.gov/hrc returned HTTP 403 to automated requests, so the URL could not be load-tested; humanrights.nh.gov is the current domain as far as we know. stateLeaveLaws: RSA 275:37-f added by 2025 c. 141:263, effective Jan. 1, 2026; both parents at the same employer share 25 hours; leave also applies in the first year after adoption.

lactationAtWorkLaw.text: Since July 1, 2025, New Hampshire employers with 6+ employees in the state, including state and local government, must give unpaid breaks of about 30 minutes for every 3 hours worked to pump, for 1 year after birth, plus a clean, private space within a reasonable walk that isn't a bathroom. stateEmployeeParentalLeave.text: New Hampshire gives permanent state employees paid family leave at no cost to them: 60% of their average weekly wage for up to 6 weeks a year, including for a birth and newborn care within a year or an adoption or foster placement. voluntaryPflInsuranceLaw.text: New Hampshire's Granite State Paid Family Leave Plan is a voluntary state plan insured by MetLife and available since Jan. 1, 2023: employers can buy group coverage, and workers whose employer doesn't offer it can buy an individual plan through a state pool with premiums capped at $5 a week, a 60-day annual enrollment window and a 7-month waiting period. The statutory benefit is 60% of average weekly wages for up to 6 weeks a year (RSA 21-I:99 to 21-I:111 and RSA 282-B; 2021 law). HB 1761 (2026), which would have expanded the program, was sent to interim study.

NJ.summary: New Jersey pays 85% of wages, up to $1,119 a week in 2026: Temporary Disability Insurance for pregnancy and recovery (typically 10 to 12 weeks), then up to 12 weeks of Family Leave Insurance to bond.
NJ.programName: New Jersey Temporary Disability Insurance (TDI) and Family Leave Insurance (FLI)
NJ.pregnancyRecoveryTypical: NJ says TDI is usually payable up to 4 weeks before your expected delivery date and up to 6 weeks after birth (8 weeks after a C-section). It can last longer if your provider certifies complications. NJ describes this as typically 10–12 weeks of TDI, followed by up to 12 weeks of FLI bonding.
NJ.wageReplacement: 85% of your average weekly wage, up to a maximum of $1,119/week in 2026 ($1,081 in 2025). The same max applies to TDI and FLI.
NJ.waitingPeriod: TDI has a 7-day 'waiting week'. NJ pays from the 8th day, and pays the first 7 days retroactively once your leave reaches 22 days, which a pregnancy claim normally does. FLI bonding has no waiting period.
NJ.jobProtection: Yes, as of July 17, 2026 (P.L.2025, c.279). If you receive TDI or FLI benefits and your leave isn't already covered by the NJ Family Leave Act, the TDI/FLI law entitles you to your same or an equivalent job when leave ends. There is no minimum employer size or work-history requirement. The NJ Family Leave Act (12 weeks of job-protected bonding leave in 24 months) now covers employers with 15+ employees, down from 30+, and employees with 3 months and 250 hours on the job, down from 12 months and 1,000 hours. Federal FMLA (50+ employees, 12 months, 1,250 hours) can also protect pregnancy and childbirth recovery.
NJ.eligibilitySummary: For 2026 claims you must have worked 20 base weeks earning at least $310/week, or earned at least $15,500 total, in the base year (first 4 of the last 5 completed quarters). Most NJ private and public employees are covered. Federal employees, out-of-state employees, and contractors who aren't employees are not; local government is optional for TDI. TDI can be paid by the state or by your employer's approved private plan. FLI bonding must be used within the child's first year.
NJ.notes: Apply for TDI after you stop working and your provider certifies you're unable to work, within 30 days of starting leave. After delivery, return Form P30 so NJ can send the FL2 for bonding. FLI bonding can be 12 consecutive weeks or 56 individual days (8 weeks) within the baby's first year. Both parents can each claim FLI. There is no combined cap: TDI (up to 26 weeks) and FLI (12 weeks) are separate. NJ's maternity FAQ confirms a mother who exhausts TDI before birth can still get up to 12 weeks of FLI. Your total TDI dollars are capped at the 'maximum benefit amount' on your approval notice, which can be less than 26 full weeks. 2026 changes effective July 17, 2026: TDI/FLI job protection, the lower NJFLA thresholds, and you may choose the order of NJ Earned Sick Leave vs. TDI/FLI but can't receive both at once. NJDOL says rulemaking may still change procedures. Some sources say the NJ Family Leave Act threshold will drop further in 2027 and 2028, but the enacted law and NJDOL's guidance show only the 15+ threshold. NJDOL hadn't published the 2027 maximum as of October 2026.

Apply for TDI after you stop working and your provider certifies you're unable to work, within 30 days of starting leave. After delivery, return Form P30 so NJ can send the FL2 for bonding. FLI bonding can be 12 consecutive weeks or 56 individual days (8 weeks) within the baby's first year. Both parents can each claim FLI. There is no combined cap: TDI (up to 26 weeks) and FLI (12 weeks) are separate, so combinedMaxWeeks is null. NJ's maternity FAQ confirms a mother who exhausts TDI before birth can still get up to 12 weeks of FLI. Your total TDI dollars are capped at the 'maximum benefit amount' on your approval notice, which can be less than 26 full weeks. 2026 changes effective July 17, 2026: TDI/FLI job protection, the lower NJFLA thresholds, and you may choose the order of NJ Earned Sick Leave vs. TDI/FLI but can't receive both at once. NJDOL says rulemaking may still change procedures. Conflicts: Mercer (Feb 2026) lists a $1,199 max and the 2025 eligibility figures ($303/week, $15,200); NJDOL's official 2026 figures are $1,119, $310 and $15,500. NPWF (Apr 2026) says NJFLA's threshold drops to 10+ employees on July 17, 2027 and 5+ on July 17, 2028. The enacted text of P.L.2025, c.279 and NJDOL's guidance show only the 15+ threshold, so treat further phase-downs as unverified. The 2027 maximum had not been published on the NJDOL pages checked.

Benefit formula (checked 2026-10-09): The rate (85% of AWW) and the 2026 max ($1,119) come from NJDOL's TDI, FLI and maternity pages. The rounding is in N.J.S.A. 43:21-40(c) as amended by P.L.2019, c.37. NJDOL's worked example: $18,200 in base-year wages over 45 base weeks gives an AWW of $404 and a weekly benefit of $343. Unrounded, 85% of $404.44 is $343.77, so the agency rounds down to the dollar. NJ's AWW is base-year earnings divided by base weeks, not the most recent pay. No statutory minimum weekly benefit; eligibility in 2026 needs 20 base weeks at $310+ or $15,500 total. waitingDays is 0 because NJ pays the TDI waiting week retroactively once leave reaches 22 days, which a normal pregnancy claim does. FLI bonding has no waiting week. The 1000 and 1500 examples are computed from the published rule.

NM.summary: New Mexico has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
NM.wageReplacement: No state paid family leave program.
NM.jobProtection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers. New Mexico's Human Rights Act (employers with 4+ employees) requires reasonable pregnancy accommodations, such as schedule changes, and bars forcing a pregnant worker onto leave if another accommodation would work.
NM.stateLeaveLaws: No state law beyond federal FMLA was found. New Mexico's Human Rights Act (employers with 4+ employees) requires reasonable pregnancy accommodations, such as schedule changes, and bars forcing a pregnant worker onto leave if another accommodation would work.
NM.notes: There's no state paid family leave program and no law for voluntary family leave insurance. Paid time off after a birth depends on your employer's own policy, short-term disability insurance if you have it, or paid sick time. Legislation: HB 11 (Paid Family and Medical Leave Act) passed the House 38-31 in February 2025, then died in the Senate; no PFML bill was filed in the 2026 session.

LFC fiscal impact report for 2025 HB 264 (Feb 2025) confirms the policy still exists via 'executive orders in 2019 and 2020' with a probationary-period restriction; HB 264 (to put it in statute) died. NY.summary: New York pays up to 12 weeks of Paid Family Leave to bond at 67% of wages (max $1,228.53 a week in 2026); disability benefits for pregnancy and recovery pay only 50%, up to $170 a week.
NY.programName: New York Paid Family Leave (PFL) and Disability Benefits Law (DBL) short-term disability
NY.pregnancyRecoveryTypical: WCB says DBL pays a pregnant worker for 4 weeks before the due date and 6 weeks after birth (8 weeks after a C-section). It can extend up to 26 weeks with documentation from your provider. PFL bonding starts after birth and can't be paid at the same time as DBL.
NY.wageReplacement: PFL (bonding): 67% of your average weekly wage, up to 67% of the NY State average weekly wage: max $1,228.53/week in 2026. DBL (your own pregnancy/childbirth disability): 50% of your average weekly wage for the last 8 weeks worked, max only $170/week.
NY.waitingPeriod: DBL: 7-day unpaid waiting period; benefits start on the 8th consecutive day of disability. PFL bonding: no waiting period.
NY.jobProtection: PFL is job-protected: after PFL you're entitled to your same or a comparable job with the same benefits and pay. The law sets no employer-size test; the 26-week/175-day eligibility rule applies. DBL time for your own pregnancy or childbirth recovery has no job protection under the DBL law, so federal FMLA (50+ employees, 12 months, 1,250 hours) is the main protection for that period. NY law also bars retaliation for taking legally protected absences.
NY.eligibilitySummary: PFL: you must be employed by a covered NY employer, working 20+ hours/week for 26 consecutive weeks or fewer than 20 hours/week for 175 days worked. Most private employers must carry DBL and PFL. Public employers and self-employed people can opt in. Construction workers under a CBA get an alternative test starting in 2027. DBL: eligible after 4 consecutive weeks with a covered employer, and you must be under the care of a physician, certified nurse midwife or other listed provider. Claims go through your employer's insurance carrier, not the state.
NY.notes: The $1,228.53 max is 67% of the 2024 New York State average weekly wage ($1,833.63). You file PFL and disability claims with your employer's insurance carrier, not the state; the disability claim form is DB-450 (https://www.wcb.ny.gov/content/main/forms/db450.pdf). The usual path for moms: DBL for about 4 weeks before plus 6–8 weeks after birth, then PFL bonding within 12 months of birth. DBL and PFL combined can't exceed 26 weeks in any 52-week period, so a 10-week DBL claim leaves the full 12 weeks of PFL (22 total). Each parent can take 12 weeks of PFL. Unchanged in 2026: the DBL max is still $170/week. Also note the separate Paid Prenatal Leave law (Labor Law § 196-b, since January 1, 2025): 20 hours of paid leave per 52 weeks for prenatal care for private-sector employees, with no minimum work requirement. WCB reported the 2025 NYS average weekly wage as $1,922.25 (April 2026). The 2027 PFL maximum is set by the Department of Financial Services.

Benefit formula (checked 2026-10-09): Top-level = PFL (bonding); medical = DBL (pregnancy/childbirth disability). PFL: 67% of AWW (average of the last 8 weeks), capped at 67% of the NYSAWW ($1,833.63, which is the 2024 NYSAWW used for 2026). Max $1,228.53 from 2026-01-01. PFL examples are from paidfamilyleave.ny.gov/2026: $519/wk gives $347.73, $1,000/wk gives $670, and the NYSAWW of $1,833.63 'or more' gives $1,228.53. That page returns 403 to curl, so I read it through WebFetch; the WCB press release was fetched directly. PFL floor (WCL 204(2)(a), nysenate.gov via WebFetch): benefit 'shall not be less than one hundred dollars per week', except that an employee earning under $100/week receives full wages, hence weeklyMin 100 + wage-if-lower. DBL: 50% of AWW, max $170 (WCL 204), with a 7-day unpaid waiting period (WCL 208). DBL can't be fully expressed: WCL 204 and form DB-820.1 say an employee whose AWW is under $20 gets their full AWW; that edge case is ignored (weeklyMin null). DBL examples are computed. The top-level waitingDays is 0 because PFL has none; the 7-day DBL wait is in medical.waitingDays. Employers may carry DBL/PFL through private insurers, and some offer richer plans, but the statutory formula is the floor. NYSAWW for 2025 ($1,922.25, WCB SN 046-1805) will drive the 2027 PFL max; it is not in effect yet.

OR.summary: Oregon pays up to 12 weeks for recovery and bonding combined, plus 2 more weeks for pregnancy (14 total), at up to 100% of wages, max $1,692.16 a week for claims from June 28, 2026.
OR.programName: Paid Leave Oregon (Oregon Paid Family and Medical Leave Insurance)
OR.wageReplacement: 100% of your average weekly wage if you earn 65% or less of the state average weekly wage; above that, 65% of the state average weekly wage plus 50% of your wages above that amount. Max $1,692.16/week for benefit years starting on or after June 28, 2026 ($1,636.56 if your benefit year started earlier); min $70.51.
OR.waitingPeriod: None (no waiting week for any leave type)
OR.jobProtection: Yes, in the Paid Leave law itself, for employees who have worked at least 90 consecutive days for the employer, at employers of any size. You get your same job back; if it no longer exists, employers with 25+ employees must offer an equivalent job (within 50 miles), and employers with fewer than 25 may give a different job with similar duties and the same pay and benefits. Health insurance continues during leave. Leave runs at the same time as federal FMLA when both apply; the Oregon Family Leave Act (OFLA, unpaid) separately covers some other reasons such as bereavement.
OR.eligibilitySummary: You must work for an employer in Oregon and have earned at least $1,000 in wages in your base year (or alternate base year), with no minimum time on the job to get benefits. Covers full-time, part-time and seasonal workers of nearly all employers. Self-employed people, independent contractors and Tribal government employers can opt in. Not covered: federal employees and some other excluded groups.
OR.notes: Weekly max did change mid-2026, but on June 28, 2026, not July 1: per the Oregon Employment Department, the max rose from $1,636.56 to $1,692.16 (min from $68.19 to $70.51) for Paid Leave claims whose benefit year begins on or after June 28, 2026; anyone whose benefit year began earlier keeps the $1,636.56 cap for that whole benefit year. Up to 12 weeks per 52-week benefit year for family, medical and safe leave combined; only the parent who gives birth can add up to 2 more weeks (14 total) for pregnancy, childbirth or related conditions including lactation. Bonding leave must be used within the first year after birth, and each parent can take their own 12 weeks. If your employer has an approved equivalent plan, you apply through that plan instead. Tell your employer at least 30 days ahead for planned leave; apply from 30 days before to 30 days after leave starts (missing written notice can cut your first payment by 25%). Job protection applies at employers of any size for employees with 90+ days of service; employers with fewer than 25 workers get more flexibility if the job no longer exists. The 2026 contribution rate is 1% of wages up to $184,500 (employees pay 60%; employers with 25+ employees pay 40%).

Tell your employer at least 30 days ahead for planned leave; apply from 30 days before to 30 days after leave starts (missing written notice can cut your first payment by 25%). Job-protection conflict: Mercer says job protection applies only at employers with 25+ employees, but ORS 657B.060 and Paid Leave Oregon say all employers must restore employees with 90+ days of service (smaller employers just get more flexibility if the job no longer exists). NPWF's eligibility text about 180 days and 25 hours/week describes older OFLA rules, not Paid Leave Oregon benefits. The 2026 contribution rate is 1% of wages up to $184,500 (employees pay 60%; employers with 25+ employees pay 40%).

Benefit formula (checked 2026-10-09): ORS 657B.050: 100% of AWW up to 65% of the SAWW, plus 50% above that; max 120% and min 5% of SAWW. SAWW = $1,410.13 for benefit years starting on or after 2026-06-28 (OED release), so the threshold is 916.5845 (kept unrounded because the agency calculator doesn't round it), the max is $1,692.16 and the min is $70.51. Benefit years that started before 2026-06-28 keep SAWW $1,363.80: threshold $886.47, max $1,636.56, min $68.19. The calculator only supports one set. Examples are the output of Paid Leave Oregon's benefits calculator: I ran its own JS (site-compiled.min.js, hidden calc_rate = 1410.13, Math.round to cents) with annual wages = AWW x 52. The calculator returns 0 when AWW is under $1,000/52 (not eligible) and the minimum when AWW is under 5% of SAWW, so the minimum is a plain floor, not wage-if-lower. OR's AWW = base-year wages / 52. No waiting week for any leave type. On weeks, the brief's '12 + 2 pregnancy weeks' structure is used: recovery 2 = the pregnancy add-on and bonding 12 = the shared balance.

a covered individual may qualify for up to two additional weeks of benefits for limitations related to pregnancy, childbirth or a related medical condition, including but not limited to lactation, for a total amount of leave ... not to exceed 14 weeks per benefit year.

If you are currently pregnant or have been pregnant, you may be able to take up to 2 additional weeks (up to 14 total weeks). Only the parent who gives birth is eligible for the additional 2 weeks of leave.

benefitFormula.explain: Oregon pays 100% of your average weekly wage up to $916.58, plus half of anything above that, between $70.51 and $1,692.16 a week. These amounts apply when your benefit year starts on or after June 28, 2026.

weeks.note: One 12-week balance per benefit year covers medical and family (bonding) leave, and only the parent who gave birth can add up to 2 more weeks for pregnancy, childbirth or related conditions, for 14 total. Oregon has no vaginal vs. C-section rule, and moving recovery time into the 12-week balance doesn't change the 14-week total.

PA.summary: Pennsylvania has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
PA.wageReplacement: No state paid family leave program.
PA.jobProtection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. No Pennsylvania law sets a required amount of pregnancy or parental leave beyond federal FMLA. State Human Relations Commission rules (employers with 4+ workers) say leave, extension and reinstatement policies must apply to pregnancy and childbirth recovery on the same terms as other temporary disabilities.
PA.stateLeaveLaws: No Pennsylvania law sets a required amount of pregnancy or parental leave beyond federal FMLA. State Human Relations Commission rules (employers with 4+ workers) say leave, extension and reinstatement policies must apply to pregnancy and childbirth recovery on the same terms as other temporary disabilities.
PA.notes: There's no state paid family leave program and no law for voluntary family leave insurance. Paid time off after a birth depends on your employer's own policy, short-term disability insurance if you have it, or paid sick time.
PA.researchNotes:
No state paid family leave program and no voluntary family leave insurance law, per NCSL (Nov 2025), Mercer (Feb 2026), NPWF (Apr 2026) and Tilt (Jul 2026). Paid time off after a birth depends on your employer's own policy, short-term disability insurance if you have it, or paid sick time. We did not re-check this state's 2026 session bill by bill, so a voluntary insurance law passed after spring 2026 can't be fully ruled out.

Workplace-law fields (checked 2026-10-09): Pregnancy: ABB (Dec. 2025) lists Pennsylvania among the 20 states without state protections and names Philadelphia and Pittsburgh local accommodation laws. PHRC regulations treat pregnancy as sex discrimination (16 Pa. Code 41.206) and require equal treatment of pregnancy disability under leave policies (41.103), but impose no accommodation duty. Bill-by-bill check: we read every General Act title for the 2025 session (60 acts) and 2026 session to date on palegis.us; none concerns pregnancy accommodation, lactation or family leave insurance (Act 9 of 2025 updated insurance terminology; Act 54 of 2025 is the CROWN Act). Tilt (Jul. 2026) reports Pennsylvania's mandatory PFML bills (House passed one in March 2026) have not become law. State employees: the paid parental leave guide says eligibility covers management/non-represented employees and union-represented employees whose union agreed to the side letter; FMLA eligibility = 12 months of continuous Commonwealth employment plus 1,250 hours (full-time) or 900 hours (part-time). Entitlement: 225/240 hours (6 weeks) for events from Oct. 15, 2020, and 300/320 hours (8 weeks) for events on or after Feb. 15, 2024; quota expires 6 months after the event. MD 530.30 (Dec. 11, 2013) sets the 6-month SPF entitlement (paid or unpaid) for employees with 1 year of service and 1,250 hours. We did not find the executive order or side letter that created the paid leave; the OA guide is the primary source used. The OA index of issuances (July 1, 2026) lists no newer leave directive.

Recheck (2026-10-09): lactationAtWorkLaw found: Commonwealth HR policy HR-WS001 (Jan. 4, 2024; agencies under the Governor) and 4 Pa. Code ch. 67c (adopted Dec. 21, 2018). No state pregnancy accommodation law or PHRC accommodation rule found beyond the existing 16 Pa. Code § 41.103 equal-treatment rule; Philadelphia and Pittsburgh have local laws. State-employee paid parental leave was already recorded.

State rules also require a nursing mothers' room in new Commonwealth-owned and leased buildings (4 Pa. Code ch. 67c, 2018). Private employers follow the federal PUMP Act.

RI.summary: Rhode Island pays about 60% of wages, up to $1,150 a week for claims from July 1, 2026: disability insurance for pregnancy and recovery, then up to 8 weeks of caregiver insurance to bond, within a 30-week yearly cap.
RI.programName: Rhode Island Temporary Disability Insurance (TDI) and Temporary Caregiver Insurance (TCI)
RI.wageReplacement: 4.62% of your wages in the highest-paid quarter of your base period (about 60% of weekly pay), up to $1,150/week for claims from July 1, 2026 ($1,103 for January to June 2026). Dependents' allowances are added on top: the greater of $20 or 7% of your rate per dependent child, up to 5, for a max of $1,552/week. The rate rises to 5.38% of high-quarter wages for benefit years starting in 2027 and 5.77% from 2028.
RI.waitingPeriod: No unpaid waiting week; the waiting-period statute (§ 28-41-12) was repealed. You must be out of work for at least 7 consecutive days to qualify for TDI (§ 28-41-11(c)).
RI.jobProtection: TCI (bonding) leave is job-protected by the TCI law itself (§ 28-41-35(f)): you return to your same or an equivalent position, and your employer must keep your health benefits during the leave. The TCI law sets no employer-size or tenure test. TDI (your own pregnancy or childbirth disability) has no job protection under the TDI law. For that time, look to the RI Parental and Family Medical Leave Act (employers with 50+ employees; full-time employees averaging 30+ hours/week with 12 consecutive months; 13 weeks in 2 calendar years) or federal FMLA.
RI.eligibilitySummary: You must have paid into TDI through RI covered employment and met a base-period earnings test tied to the RI minimum wage ($16.00/hour in 2026). That means either $19,200 in base-period wages, or $3,200 in one quarter plus total base-period wages of at least 1.5 times your highest quarter and at least $6,400. TCI bonding is for a newborn, adopted or foster child, and you must give your employer 30 days' written notice when possible. Private plans are not allowed in RI.
RI.notes: Apply by phone at (401) 462-8420. For claims from July 1, 2026 the maximum is $1,150 a week ($1,552 with 5 dependents); it was $1,103 for claims from January to June 2026. TDI lasts up to 30 weeks and TCI up to 8. Confirmed from statute: TCI bonding rose from 7 to 8 weeks on January 1, 2026 (§ 28-41-35(d)(5)); TDI and TCI together are capped at 30 times your weekly rate per benefit year; pregnancy and childbirth are covered like any other TDI sickness (§ 28-41-8). Laws effective January 1, 2026 also added siblings and organ/bone-marrow donation to TCI and raised the dependents' allowance minimum to $20. Upcoming: the benefit rate rises to 5.38% (about 70% of pay) in 2027 and 5.77% (about 75%) in 2028. A birthing mom typically claims TDI for pregnancy and recovery, then TCI for bonding. TCI and TDI can't be paid at the same time for the same purpose, and TCI counts toward the 30-week combined cap. The statute sets no TDI duration in weeks; 30 weeks is the 30-times-rate cap, also limited to 36% of base-period wages.
RI.researchNotes:
The 2026 weekly maximum comes from DLT's July 1, 2026 quick reference PDF ($1,150; $1,552 with 5 dependents; TDI 30 weeks, TCI 8 weeks; apply by phone at (401) 462-8420). DLT's HTML pages (overview, FAQ, apply) show a 'verify you are human' check that we did not bypass, so DLT's typical pregnancy-recovery guidance and an online apply link are not confirmed. applyUrl is null, and infoUrl is DLT's TDI/TCI program page (NPWF cites its subpages; the page itself returned the CAPTCHA, so we could not open it). NPWF (Apr 2026) and Mercer (Feb 2026) list $1,103, the maximum for claims before July 1, 2026. Confirmed from statute: TCI bonding rose from 7 to 8 weeks on January 1, 2026 (§ 28-41-35(d)(5)); TDI and TCI together are capped at 30 times your weekly rate per benefit year; pregnancy and childbirth are covered like any other TDI sickness (§ 28-41-8). Laws effective January 1, 2026 also added siblings and organ/bone-marrow donation to TCI and raised the dependents' allowance minimum to $20. Upcoming: the benefit rate rises to 5.38% (about 70% of pay) in 2027 and 5.77% (about 75%) in 2028. A birthing mom typically claims TDI for pregnancy and recovery, then TCI for bonding. TCI and TDI can't be paid at the same time for the same purpose, and TCI counts toward the 30-week combined cap. The statute sets no TDI duration in weeks; 30 weeks is the 30-times-rate cap, also limited to 36% of base-period wages.

Benefit formula (checked 2026-10-09): R.I. Gen. Laws 28-41-5 (version effective 2026-01-01): 4.62% of HQW for benefit years before 2027-01-01 (5.38% in 2027, 5.77% from 2028), applied directly to the quarter's wages with no divisor. The individual rate is raised to the next whole dollar. The max is 85% of the prior-year AWW, also raised to the next dollar: 85% x $1,352.74 = $1,149.83, so $1,150. The DLT quick reference effective 2026-07-01 lists min $148 and max $1,150 per week; the max was $1,103 for benefit years beginning 2026-01-01 to 06-30. The $148 minimum equals 4.62% of the $3,200 minimum qualifying quarter, rounded up, so every eligible claimant already gets at least $148. TCI (bonding) pays the same rate. Not expressible: the dependents' allowance (the greater of $20 or 7% of the rate per child, up to 5, rounded down; max with 5 dependents $1,552) is added on top; flag it in the UI. No waiting period since 2012, though you must be out at least 7 consecutive days. DLT has no worked example that we could load (dlt.ri.gov HTML pages return 403 to curl and WebFetch), so all 3 examples are computed from the statute. Implementation trap: 0.0462 x 10000 = 462.00000000000006 in floating point, so round to cents before applying dollar-up, or the result comes out $463. The 6/8-week recovery split is not from a DLT page.

benefitFormula.explain: Rhode Island pays 4.62% of what you earned in your highest-paid quarter (about 60% of your weekly pay), rounded up to the dollar, between $148 and $1,150 a week. Each dependent child adds at least $20 a week.

weeks.note: TDI pays for as long as your provider certifies you can't work. DLT publishes no vaginal vs. C-section schedule we could load, so recovery uses the usual 6/8-week certification. TCI adds up to 8 weeks of bonding in 2026, and TDI plus TCI can't exceed 30 times your weekly rate per benefit year.

SC.summary: South Carolina has no state paid family leave program. A 2024 law lets insurers sell paid family leave policies to employers, so you're covered only if your employer buys one.
SC.wageReplacement: Set by each policy; only if your employer buys coverage.
SC.waitingPeriod: Set by each policy (the law only requires the policy to say whether there is an unpaid waiting period).
SC.jobProtection: This law does not protect your job. The federal FMLA may: up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if your employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you have worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers.
SC.eligibilitySummary: Only employees (people for whom the employer completes a Form I-9; not independent contractors) whose employer buys a family leave insurance policy or rider; eligibility rules are set by the policy. No state-run program.
SC.lawCitation: Paid Family Leave Insurance Act, S.C. Code §§ 38-103-10 to 38-103-90; 2024 Act No. 206 (H.4832), effective May 21, 2024
SC.policyRequirements: Family leave insurance can be an amendment or rider to a group disability income or life policy, included in one, or a separate group policy bought by an employer. It may cover caring for a family member with a serious health condition; bonding with a child in the first 12 months after birth, adoption or foster placement; FMLA military qualifying exigencies; caring for a family service member injured in the line of duty; and other leave the policy lists. The policy must provide at least 2 weeks of benefits for each covered reason in a 52-consecutive-week period, and must state the benefit amount, the wage definition, any unpaid waiting period and any offsets. The Department of Insurance reports on use each year.
SC.stateLeaveLaws: No state law beyond federal FMLA was found.
SC.notes: These laws only allow insurers to sell family leave insurance to employers. They do not cover your own recovery from pregnancy or childbirth, which is paid (if at all) by short-term disability insurance, and there is no state agency to apply to; claims go to the insurer named on your employer's policy. The Department of Insurance's first report (Dec. 31, 2024) found six companies offering stand-alone or rider products, none of which had sold any, and said the active coverage appears to sit inside disability income or life policies. We did not find the report due Jan. 1, 2026.
SC.researchNotes: Workplace-law fields (checked 2026-10-09): NEW in 2026: Act 249 (S. 11), ratified June 29, 2026, approved June 30, 2026, effective Oct. 1, 2026 for qualifying events on or after that date. It raises the non-birth parent's paid leave from 2 to 4 weeks, adds stillbirth, broadens 'eligible state employee' (positions eligible to earn annual leave, incl. four-year and technical college employees), and raises adoption leave (§ 8-11-155) to 6 weeks for the primary caregiver and 4 for the other parent. The online S.C. Code (current through the 2025 session) still shows the 2022 version (6 and 2 weeks); we used the ratified act text. § 8-11-151 (2023 Act 17) gives school district employees leave 'to the same extent available to employees of the State pursuant to Section 8-11-150', so they should follow the new 6/4 split, but we did not see a separate statement confirming it. CONFLICT: NCSL's PFML table says South Carolina state workers 'can access up to 12 weeks of parental leave'; the statute and Act 249 show 6 weeks (birth parent) and 4 weeks (other parent), so we followed the statute. 2025-2026 check: scstatehouse.gov legislation search for 'family leave insurance', 'paid family leave' and 'pregnancy accommodations' found no Session 126 bills; 'lactation' found only insurance-coverage bills (S. 42, H. 3243, H. 3108). Chapter 38-103 history shows only 2024 Act 206. The lactation law took effect for employers 30 days after the Human Affairs Commission posted guidance (2020 Act 141, Sections 4-5).

The policy of insurance must set forth the length of family leave benefits that are available for each covered family leave reason, which will in no event be less than two weeks during a period of fifty-two consecutive calendar weeks.
All six companies have reported that they have not sold any products/riders in South Carolina for this benefit, though the coverage appears to be available.

pregnancyAccommodationLaw.text: South Carolina's Pregnancy Accommodations Act (2018) requires employers with 15+ employees to make reasonable accommodations for medical needs from pregnancy, childbirth or related conditions, including lactation, unless it causes undue hardship. Examples include more frequent breaks, seating, help with lifting, a temporary transfer and schedule changes, and employers must give workers written notice of these rights (S.C. Code §§ 1-13-30, 1-13-80).

lactationAtWorkLaw.text: South Carolina's Lactation Support Act (2020) covers every employer with 1+ employees, including state and local government: it must give reasonable unpaid break time, or let you use paid breaks or meal time, to pump each day, and make reasonable efforts to provide a private place near your work area that isn't a toilet stall. An employer doesn't have to provide break time if it would cause undue hardship (S.C. Code § 41-1-130).

stateEmployeeParentalLeave.text: South Carolina state employees who give birth (including a stillbirth) get 6 weeks of paid leave at 100% of base pay, used within 12 months; the other parent gets 4 weeks for births on or after Oct. 1, 2026, up from 2. The benefit started in 2022 (S.C. Code § 8-11-150), public school district employees got it to the same extent in 2023 (§ 8-11-151), and Act 249 of 2026 raised the second parent's weeks.

voluntaryPflInsuranceLaw.text: South Carolina's Paid Family Leave Insurance Act lets life and disability income insurers sell family leave coverage to employers as a rider to, or part of, a group disability or life policy, or as a separate group policy. Covered reasons include bonding in the first 12 months after a birth, adoption or foster placement, and policies must pay at least 2 weeks per covered reason in a 52-week period. It took effect May 21, 2024 (S.C. Code §§ 38-103-10 to 38-103-90; Act 206 of 2024, H.4832).

TN.summary: Tennessee has no state paid family leave program. A 2023 law lets insurers sell paid family leave policies to employers, so you're covered only if your employer buys one.
TN.wageReplacement: Set by each policy; only if your employer buys coverage.
TN.waitingPeriod: Set by each policy (the law only requires the policy to say whether there is an unpaid waiting period).
TN.jobProtection: This law does not protect your job. The federal FMLA may: up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if your employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you have worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. Tennessee's Parental Leave Act lets full-time employees at a job site with 100+ full-time workers take up to 4 months of leave for pregnancy, childbirth, nursing an infant or adoption, after 12 consecutive months. Pay is the employer's choice. Give 3 months' notice (medical emergencies excepted) to keep your right to return.
TN.eligibilitySummary: Only employees (people for whom the employer completes a Form I-9; not independent contractors) whose employer buys a family leave insurance policy or rider; eligibility rules are set by the policy. No state-run program.
TN.lawCitation: Tennessee Paid Family Leave Insurance Act, Tenn. Code Ann. Title 56, Chapter 7 (new part); 2023 Public Chapter No. 91 (SB 454 / HB 609, 113th General Assembly), signed March 31, 2023; effective Jan. 1, 2024 for policies entered into, amended or renewed on or after that date
TN.policyRequirements: Creates paid family leave insurance as a new line that life or disability income insurers may issue to an employer, as an amendment or rider to (or part of) a group disability income or life policy, or as a separate group policy. It replaces part of income lost due to the birth or adoption of a child, foster placement, caring for a family member with a serious health condition, or a family member's active military duty or call to duty. The policy must set out the details and requirements for each covered reason. The statute sets NO minimum number of weeks or benefit amount; the Commissioner of Commerce and Insurance may adopt rules (not reviewed).
TN.stateLeaveLaws: Tennessee's Parental Leave Act lets full-time employees at a job site with 100+ full-time workers take up to 4 months of leave for pregnancy, childbirth, nursing an infant or adoption, after 12 consecutive months. Pay is the employer's choice. Give 3 months' notice (medical emergencies excepted) to keep your right to return.
TN.notes: These laws only allow insurers to sell family leave insurance to employers. They do not cover your own recovery from pregnancy or childbirth, which is paid (if at all) by short-term disability insurance, and there is no state agency to apply to; claims go to the insurer named on your employer's policy. The state's employer tax incentive for family leave insurance covered only the 2024 and 2025 tax years and has expired.

pregnancyAccommodationLaw.text: Tennessee requires employers with 15 or more employees to make reasonable accommodations for medical needs arising from pregnancy, childbirth or related conditions unless it causes undue hardship, such as more frequent breaks, lifting limits or a temporary transfer. lactationAtWorkLaw.text: Tennessee requires employers to give reasonable unpaid break time each day to pump for an infant, unless it would unduly disrupt operations, and to make reasonable efforts to provide a private place near the work area that isn't a toilet stall (Tenn. Code 50-1-305). Employers with 15 or more workers may also have to provide a private, non-bathroom space to pump as a pregnancy accommodation (2020).

stateEmployeeParentalLeave.text: Tennessee gives full-time state employees with at least 12 straight months of service 6 weeks of paid leave at 100% of salary after a birth or adoption, without using their sick or annual leave. It must be used within 12 months (2023 Tenn. Pub. Acts ch. 216, effective July 1, 2023).

voluntaryPflInsuranceLaw.text: Tennessee lets insurers sell paid family leave insurance to employers, either as a rider on group disability or life coverage or as a separate group policy. TX.summary: Texas has no state paid family leave program. A 2023 law lets insurers sell paid family leave policies to employers, so you're covered only if your employer buys one.
TX.wageReplacement: Set by each policy; only if your employer buys coverage.
TX.waitingPeriod: Set by each policy (the law only requires the policy to say whether there is an unpaid waiting period).
TX.jobProtection: This law does not protect your job. The federal FMLA may: up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if your employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you have worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers.
TX.eligibilitySummary: Only employees whose employer buys a group family leave insurance policy or rider; eligibility rules are set by the policy. No state-run program.
TX.lawCitation: Tex. Ins. Code Chapter 1255 (Group Family Leave Insurance); Acts 2023, 88th Leg., R.S., Ch. 703 (H.B. 1996), eff. Sept. 1, 2023
TX.policyRequirements: Applies to family leave insurance policies, or amendments or riders to group disability policies, issued in Texas by life, health and accident insurers; it counts as disability income insurance. Covered reasons can include caring for a family member with a serious health condition; bonding with a child in the first 12 months after birth, adoption or foster placement; FMLA military qualifying exigencies; caring for a family member injured in the line of duty; and other leave the policy lists. Benefits must last at least 2 weeks for each covered reason in a 52-consecutive-week period. The policy must state the benefit amount, the wage definition, any unpaid waiting period and offsets, and each covered employee gets a certificate of insurance.
TX.stateLeaveLaws: No state law beyond federal FMLA was found.
TX.notes: These laws only allow insurers to sell family leave insurance to employers. They do not cover your own recovery from pregnancy or childbirth, which is paid (if at all) by short-term disability insurance, and there is no state agency to apply to; claims go to the insurer named on your employer's policy.

Texas had no 2026 regular session. Gov't Code 661.9125 counts days without saying workdays or calendar days, so we did not convert to weeks. ABB (Dec. 2025) lists Texas among the 20 states without statewide protections because its law covers only municipal and county employers. TWC's Civil Rights Division enforces Labor Code ch. 21 (pregnancy discrimination) and links to the PWFA for accommodation requests.

pregnancyAccommodationLaw.text: Texas requires cities and counties to make a reasonable effort to accommodate an employee whose doctor finds her partially restricted by pregnancy, and to give her an available temporary assignment in the same office if she can't do her regular job. The law covers only city and county employees, not private employers (Tex. Local Gov't Code § 180.004, 2001).

lactationAtWorkLaw.text: Texas requires public employers (state agencies, public colleges, cities, counties, school districts and other local governments) to give reasonable break time and a private place, other than a multi-user bathroom, to pump, and to adopt a written lactation policy (Tex. Gov't Code ch. 619, 2015). Private employers aren't required to; they can choose to earn the state's "mother-friendly" designation (Tex. Health & Safety Code § 165.003).

stateEmployeeParentalLeave.text: Texas gives state employees 40 days of paid leave after giving birth, and 20 days after a spouse's birth, a surrogate birth or an adoption, taken during their FMLA leave. It covers executive-branch agency employees (not public colleges and universities) and other Employees Retirement System members (Tex. Gov't Code § 661.9125, 2023). Employees not yet eligible for FMLA can take up to 12 weeks of parental leave, unpaid once accrued leave runs out (§ 661.913).

voluntaryPflInsuranceLaw.text: A 2023 law lets insurers sell family leave insurance to employers, as a separate policy or a rider to group disability coverage, with at least 2 weeks of benefits per covered reason in a year. You're covered only if your employer buys a policy (Tex. Ins. Code ch. 1255, effective Sept. 1, 2023).

UT.summary: Utah has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
UT.wageReplacement: No state paid family leave program.
UT.jobProtection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers.
UT.stateLeaveLaws: No state law beyond federal FMLA was found.
UT.notes: There's no state paid family leave program and no law for voluntary family leave insurance. Paid time off after a birth depends on your employer's own policy, short-term disability insurance if you have it, or paid sick time. Legislation: No paid family leave or family leave insurance bills for private workers were found in the 2026 session.

Legislation: No paid family leave or family leave insurance bills for private workers were found in the 2026 session.

pregnancyAccommodationLaw.text: Utah requires employers with 15 or more employees, plus state and local government, to provide reasonable accommodations for pregnancy, childbirth, breastfeeding and related conditions unless it would cause undue hardship. Employers can't demand a doctor's note for more frequent restroom, food or water breaks (Utah Code § 34A-5-106, 2016).

lactationAtWorkLaw.text: Utah requires public employers (state executive-branch agencies, cities, counties, school districts and public colleges) to give breastfeeding employees reasonable pump breaks for at least a year after birth, plus a clean, private room with an electrical outlet that isn't a bathroom and access to a refrigerator (Utah Code § 34-49-202, 2015). Private employers with 15 or more employees must reasonably accommodate breastfeeding under the state's 2016 pregnancy accommodation law.

stateEmployeeParentalLeave.text: Utah gives benefits-eligible state employees in the executive, legislative and judicial branches (not public colleges) 3 work weeks of paid parental leave after a birth, adoption or guardianship. An employee who gives birth first gets up to 6 work weeks of paid postpartum recovery leave, up from 3 weeks before July 1, 2026, for up to 9 paid weeks in all (Utah Code § 63A-17-511; enacted 2022, expanded by H.B. 329 in 2026).

voluntaryPflInsuranceLaw.text: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026. Bills to add family leave insurance to Utah's insurance code failed in 2024 and 2025.

VT.summary: Vermont has no required paid leave. The voluntary VT FMLI plan pays 60% of wages for up to 6 weeks if your employer buys it or you enroll yourself (enroll in May; benefits start the next January).
VT.programName: Vermont Family and Medical Leave Insurance (VT FMLI), insured and administered by The Hartford
VT.wageReplacement: 60% of your average weekly wage up to a maximum weekly benefit tied to the Social Security wage base; max $2,128.85/week for 2026 claims under the state-employee plan. The Hartford's individual-plan page still lists $2,031.92. Only if you are enrolled: through an employer that buys VT FMLI, or by buying individual coverage yourself. Employer plans can offer 60-70%.
VT.waitingPeriod: 7 calendar days at the start of each claim, waived when bonding leave immediately follows a childbirth medical claim. Individual plan: enroll May 1-31, coverage starts July 1, then a 6-month eligibility waiting period, so benefits are first available the following January 1.
VT.jobProtection: VT FMLI pays benefits only; it does not protect your job. Separate laws may: Vermont's Parental and Family Leave Act (21 V.S.A. § 472) gives up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected parental leave a year (including pregnancy and, since July 1, 2025, recovery from childbirth or miscarriage) at employers with 10+ employees for employees with 1 year at an average of 30+ hours/week; the federal FMLA also applies at employers with 50+ employees.
VT.eligibilitySummary: Voluntary. State of Vermont employees are covered by the state plan. Employers with a Vermont location and 2+ employees may buy group coverage (they design it: 6-26 weeks, 60-70% pay). Individuals can buy the 6-week individual plan if they live and work in Vermont and their employer doesn't offer FMLI, or if they are a self-employed Vermont resident; one-employee employers also use the individual pool. Annual enrollment is May 1-31; special enrollment within 30 days of losing employer coverage, changing jobs, or moving to Vermont.
VT.stateLeaveLaws: Vermont's Parental and Family Leave Act gives up to 12 weeks a year of unpaid, job-protected leave for pregnancy, recovery from childbirth or miscarriage, and bonding with a new child in its first year, at employers with 10+ employees who work an average of 30+ hours a week. You qualify after 1 year with the employer averaging 30+ hours a week; your benefits continue and you get the same or a comparable job back (21 V.S.A. §§ 471-472; childbirth and miscarriage recovery added by Act 32 of 2025).
VT.notes: Phase 3 confirmed: the individual purchasing pool opened with enrollment May 1-31, 2025, coverage effective July 1, 2025, and benefits from Jan. 1, 2026 (Governor's release and The Hartford). Earlier phases: state employees (benefits July 1, 2023) and employers with 2+ employees (July 1, 2024). For a pregnant mom buying individually, timing is tight: enrolling in May 2026 means benefits only from Jan. 1, 2027. Weeks are a combined 6 per 52-week benefit year for all leave types under the individual and state-employee plans, so recovery from childbirth plus bonding share the same 6 weeks. Employer group plans can provide more (6-26 weeks). The Hartford lists a $2,128.85 cap for 2026 claims on the state-employee plan, but its individual-plan page still shows the 2025 figure ($2,031.92), so individual buyers should confirm with The Hartford. VT FMLI comes from a governor's initiative and a state contract, not a law. 2026 legislature: Vermont did NOT enact a mandatory paid family leave program. The only leave-related act of the 2025-2026 biennium is Act 32 (H.461, signed May 22, 2025, effective July 1, 2025), which expands UNPAID leave under the Parental and Family Leave Act, and no paid-leave bill appears on the 2026 bills-passed lists.

Phase 3 confirmed: the individual purchasing pool opened with enrollment May 1-31, 2025, coverage effective July 1, 2025, and benefits from Jan. 1, 2026 (Governor's release and The Hartford). Earlier phases: state employees (benefits July 1, 2023) and employers with 2+ employees (July 1, 2024). For a pregnant mom buying individually, timing is tight: enrolling in May 2026 means benefits only from Jan. 1, 2027. Weeks are a combined 6 per 52-week benefit year for all leave types under the individual and state-employee plans, so recovery from childbirth plus bonding share the same 6 weeks. Employer group plans can provide more (6-26 weeks). CONFLICT on the 2026 cap: The Hartford's state-employee plan lists $2,128.85 for 2026 claims (60% of the 2026 SS wage base / 52), but its individual-plan page and FAQ still list $2,031.92 (the 2025 figure). Individual buyers should confirm with The Hartford. The only leave-related act of the 2025-2026 biennium is Act 32 (H.461, signed May 22, 2025, effective July 1, 2025), which expands UNPAID leave under the Parental and Family Leave Act, and no paid-leave bill appears on the 2026 bills-passed lists.

pregnancyAccommodationLaw.text: Since Jan. 1, 2018, every Vermont employer with at least 1 employee must provide reasonable accommodations for pregnancy-related conditions unless it would cause undue hardship, using the same standards as disability accommodations, and must post a notice of the law (21 V.S.A. § 495k; Act 21 of 2017).

lactationAtWorkLaw.text: For 3 years after a birth, every Vermont employer must give nursing employees reasonable time during the day to pump (paid or unpaid, at the employer's choice) and a private space that isn't a bathroom stall. An employer can be exempted only if this would substantially disrupt its operations (21 V.S.A. § 305, enacted 2008).

stateEmployeeParentalLeave.text: State of Vermont employees (classified or exempt, in the executive, judicial and legislative branches) with at least 1 year of service are automatically enrolled in VT FMLI, which pays 60% of base weekly wages for up to 6 combined weeks a year, including for childbirth recovery and bonding with a new child. The state pays the full premium, and benefits began July 1, 2023.

voluntaryPflInsuranceLaw.text: Vermont's voluntary plan, VT FMLI, insured by The Hartford, was created by Gov. Phil Scott's administration through a state contract rather than a statute. It covered state employees from July 2023, employers with 2+ employees could buy plans from July 2024 (6-26 weeks at 60-70% pay), and individuals and self-employed Vermonters could enroll from 2025, with benefits from Jan. 1, 2026. The 2025-2026 legislature passed no paid leave law; its only leave act (Act 32 of 2025) expanded unpaid leave.

VA.summary: Virginia passed paid family and medical leave in April 2026, but benefits don't start until December 1, 2028: up to 12 weeks a year at 80% of wages.
VA.programName: Virginia Paid Family and Medical Leave Insurance Program (PFML), administered by the Virginia Employment Commission
VA.wageReplacement: When benefits start Dec. 1, 2028: 80% of your average weekly wage (your full wage if you earn under $100/week), min $100/week, max equal to 100% of the state average weekly wage, set each year. The 2028 dollar cap hasn't been published. No benefits are paid in 2026.
VA.waitingPeriod: None for employees (benefits payable from the first day you're eligible in a benefit year). Self-employed people who opt in more than 26 weeks after becoming self-employed must wait 52 weeks before benefits are paid.
VA.jobProtection: Yes, in the new law: if you've worked for your current employer at least 120 days before leave, you must be restored to your job or one with equivalent seniority, status, pay, benefits and service credits, and health coverage continues during leave. Retaliation, including immigration-status threats, is prohibited. Until benefits begin in Dec. 2028, only federal FMLA (50+ employees, 12 months/1,250 hours) gives job-protected leave.
VA.eligibilitySummary: You'll need to meet Virginia's minimum earnings test for unemployment insurance (wages in your two highest base-period quarters at least the lowest amount in the UI benefit table, earned in at least 2 quarters) and be authorized to work in the U.S. Covers nearly all private and local-government employers, including small businesses (10 or fewer employees don't pay the employer share). State employees get equal or better leave through state HR policy instead. Self-employed people can opt in for at least 3 years.
VA.notes: Confirmed enacted: HB 1207 (2026 Va. Acts ch. 1093) and SB 2 (ch. 981) were both approved April 22, 2026, at the reconvened session with the Governor's substitute. They're codified at Va. Code 60.2-800 to 60.2-818, and VEC says Governor Spanberger and the General Assembly enacted the program April 22, 2026. Key dates (Va. Code 60.2-801 and VEC): program set up by Jan. 1, 2028; contribution rate set by Oct. 1, 2027; payroll contributions begin April 1, 2028; claims and benefits begin Dec. 1, 2028. Wage cap: contributions aren't due on wages above the Social Security contribution and benefit base (Va. Code 60.2-806(G)). Employers with more than 10 employees deduct up to 50% from pay and remit the full contribution; employers with 10 or fewer remit only the employee half. The benefit max is 100% of the state average weekly wage under Va. Code 65.2-500(B), adjusted by Sept. 30 each year for the next Jan. 1. Up to 12 weeks per benefit year for all reasons combined; 'serious health condition' expressly includes pregnancy and recovery from childbirth, so pregnancy recovery and bonding share the 12 weeks. Bonding must be in the child's first year. Safety leave is capped at 4 weeks. The earnings test is tied to Virginia's unemployment benefit table, so the 2028 dollar threshold isn't set yet. Older voluntary law: since 2022 (Acts cc. 131, 132; Va. Code 38.2-107.2), insurers may sell employers group 'family leave insurance' (renamed 'private family leave insurance' in 2026) as a rider or a separate policy. It's optional and the law sets no benefit level or duration, so it only helps if your employer bought it. Employers may use an approved private plan for the new program.

WA.summary: Washington pays up to 12 weeks to bond plus medical leave for pregnancy and recovery, up to 16 weeks combined (18 with a complication such as a C-section), at up to 90% of wages, max $1,647 a week in 2026.
WA.programName: Washington Paid Family and Medical Leave
WA.pregnancyRecoveryTypical: Washington automatically treats the first 6 weeks after you give birth (the 'postnatal period') as medical leave. You don't need a medical certification and there's no waiting week, just proof of birth. Leave before birth for pregnancy incapacity needs a medical certification and has a waiting week. You can then add family leave to bond, up to 16 weeks total, or 18 if you had a pregnancy complication causing incapacity (ESD's examples are bed rest or a C-section).
WA.wageReplacement: 90% of your average weekly wage up to half the state average weekly wage, plus 50% of the amount above that. Minimum $100/week; maximum $1,647/week in 2026 ($1,542 in 2025). Your max is locked in for the claim year you start.
WA.waitingPeriod: No waiting week for bonding leave or for leave taken in the 6-week postnatal period. Medical leave taken before birth, for example pregnancy bed rest, has a 7-day unpaid waiting week.
WA.jobProtection: The PFML law itself protects your job (RCW 50A.35.010) if you've worked for your employer at least 180 calendar days and it has 25 or more employees in 2026. That threshold drops to 15+ in 2027 and 8+ from 2028; there's no hours requirement. Your employer must restore you to the same or an equivalent job and, starting 2026, keep your health coverage. Exceptions: the top 10% of salaried earners (if restoring them would cause serious financial harm and they get notice), and jobs that would not have existed anyway. Without PFML job protection, federal FMLA or other laws may apply.
WA.eligibilitySummary: You must have worked 820 hours in Washington in your qualifying period, normally the first 4 of the last 5 completed calendar quarters. If that doesn't get you to 820 hours, ESD uses the last 4 completed quarters before you apply instead. Full-time, part-time, temporary and seasonal work all count, and you don't need to be currently employed. Workers at businesses of all sizes are covered. Not covered: federal employees, tribal-business employees on tribal land, workers on an approved employer voluntary plan (who apply through that plan), and self-employed people who haven't opted in.
WA.notes: Apply within 30 days after the birth. Give your employer 30 days' notice if the leave is foreseeable. You can't get the postnatal-period approval before the baby is born. 2026 changes (HB 1213, 2025 c 304): job protection widened from 50+ employees with 12 months and 1,250 hours to 25+ employees with 180 days and no hours test; health coverage must continue for job-protected workers; employers may count FMLA time against PFML job protection with written notice; you must claim at least 4 consecutive hours per week. ESD announced on June 10, 2026 that the maximum weekly benefit will be $1,727 for new claims filed on or after January 1, 2027. Each parent can take bonding leave, and bonding must be within 12 months of the birth.
WA.researchNotes:
Apply within 30 days after the birth. Give your employer 30 days' notice if the leave is foreseeable. You can't get the postnatal-period approval before the baby is born. 2026 changes (HB 1213, 2025 c 304): job protection widened from 50+ employees with 12 months and 1,250 hours to 25+ employees with 180 days and no hours test; health coverage must continue for job-protected workers; employers may count FMLA time against PFML job protection with written notice; you must claim at least 4 consecutive hours per week. By statute the 2027 maximum is set by September 30 and takes effect January 1, but it was not found on the paidleave.wa.gov pages checked on 2026-10-09. Each parent can take bonding leave, and bonding must be within 12 months of the birth. NPWF and Mercer agree with the official durations; Mercer's 2026 max of $1,647 matches ESD.

Benefit formula (checked 2026-10-09): RCW 50A.15.020(5)-(6): 90% of AWW up to half the SAWW, plus 50% above that, rounded down to the dollar. The max is 90% of the SAWW, and the min is $100 or full wages if under $100. 2026 SAWW is $1,830 (ESD release), so the half-SAWW threshold is $915 and the max is $1,647 for claims filed on or after 2026-01-01. Examples are ESD's 2026 calculator output: I ran the BenefitsCalculator function from paidleave.wa.gov's theme bundle (AWW = floor(2 x quarter / 26); <100 gives full wage; <=915 gives max(100, floor(0.9 x AWW)); else floor(823.5 + 0.5 x (AWW - 915)); >=2562 gives 1647) with quarterly wages = AWW x 13. ESD floors AWW to the dollar before applying the formula; integer AWW inputs avoid any difference. WA's AWW = the two highest quarters / 26. waitingDays 0: per RCW 50A.15.020(1)(a) and ESD, birth and bonding leave and the 6-week postnatal period have no waiting week; prenatal medical leave such as bed rest does. UPDATE vs. the existing JSON note: ESD has now announced the 2027 max of $1,727 for claims filed on or after 2027-01-01 (2025 SAWW $1,919), at https://esd.wa.gov/about-us/news-release/2026/new-average-annual-wage-estimates-adjust-unemployment-insurance-and-paid-leave-benefits. It is not in effect yet. The 6/8 vs. 10/10 recovery/bonding split is our reading of the 16/18-week caps; the totals (16 and 18) are what ESD states.

weeks.note: The first 6 weeks after birth count as medical leave automatically, with no certification and no waiting week. WV.summary: West Virginia has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
WV.wageReplacement: No state paid family leave program.
WV.jobProtection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers.
WV.stateLeaveLaws: No state law beyond federal FMLA was found.
WV.notes: There's no state paid family leave program and no law for voluntary family leave insurance. Paid time off after a birth depends on your employer's own policy, short-term disability insurance if you have it, or paid sick time. Legislation: 2026 bills HB 5080, HB 5083 and SB 114 (paid parental leave pilot) were still pending when the session ended.
WV.researchNotes:
No state paid family leave program and no voluntary family leave insurance law, per NCSL (Nov 2025), Mercer (Feb 2026), NPWF (Apr 2026) and Tilt (Jul 2026). Paid time off after a birth depends on your employer's own policy, short-term disability insurance if you have it, or paid sick time. Legislation: 2026 bills HB 5080, HB 5083 and SB 114 (paid parental leave pilot) were still pending when the session ended.

WI.summary: Wisconsin has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
WI.wageReplacement: No state paid family leave program.
WI.jobProtection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. Wisconsin's Family and Medical Leave Act lets employees of employers with 50+ permanent workers take up to 6 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for a birth (starting within 16 weeks), plus up to 2 weeks for their own serious health condition. You need 52 weeks on the job and 1,000 hours. Give reasonable advance notice.
